  <script type="application/ld+json">
  {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "FAQPage",
    "mainEntity": [
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What is a small business set-aside?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "A small business set-aside is a federal acquisition that's restricted so only small businesses can compete. Authorized by the Small Business Act and implemented through SBA's program rules, set-asides exist because the federal government has a statutory goal to award at least 23% of all prime contract dollars to small businesses each year. Set-asides come in several flavors: total small business set-aside (any small business), 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB / EDWOSB, and SDVOSB. Certified SDVOSBs can compete for federal-wide SDVOSB set-asides; VOSB-specific set-asides are principally associated with the VA's Vets First program."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What's the difference between 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, and SDVOSB?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "The 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB / EDWOSB, and SDVOSB programs are reserved for specific categories of small business and require formal certification for program set-aside awards. Certified SDVOSBs can compete for SDVOSB set-asides and sole-source awards across the federal government. SBA also certifies VOSBs through VetCert, but VOSB-specific set-aside and sole-source authority is principally associated with the VA's Vets First program."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "How do I know if I qualify as a small business?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "SBA publishes size standards by NAICS code at sba.gov. Receipts-based size standards generally use average annual receipts over the five most recently completed fiscal years. Employee-based size standards generally use the average number of employees over the preceding completed 24 calendar months. If your business is under the threshold for a given NAICS code, you're a small business under that code. You can be small under one NAICS and large under another."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "What is the Rule of Two?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "The Rule of Two requires contracting officers to set aside an acquisition for small business participation if the CO has a reasonable expectation that offers will be received from at least two responsible small business concerns AND that award will be made at fair market prices. The rule is not optional. If both prongs are met, the CO is required to set aside the acquisition. The Rule of Two is the primary engine that drives small business set-aside volume across the federal government."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Do I have to recertify my small business size during contract performance?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "Yes, in several situations. SBA requires size recertification at the end of the fifth year of long-term contracts, before exercising any option that extends performance more than five years from contract award, and after a merger, acquisition, or change in ownership. You also must recertify your size in your SAM record at least annually. If you grow above the size threshold during performance, you may lose set-aside-eligible award status on future task orders or option exercises, depending on the contract structure."
        }
      },
      {
        "@type": "Question",
        "name": "Can I self-certify as a WOSB or SDVOSB?",
        "acceptedAnswer": {
          "@type": "Answer",
          "text": "No, not for set-aside awards. As of October 2020, WOSB and EDWOSB self-certification is no longer accepted for set-aside awards; you need SBA certification through certify.SBA.gov or an approved third-party certifier. As of 2023, SDVOSB and VOSB certification moved from the VA's Center for Verification and Evaluation (CVE) to SBA, also requiring formal certification for set-aside awards. HUBZone and 8(a) have always required formal SBA certification. The only socio-economic representation that's still self-certified for general representation purposes is small disadvantaged business (SDB), and SDB by itself does not qualify you for an 8(a) set-aside."
        }
      }
    ]
  }

}
#cfm-drawer.cfm-mode-cco .cfm-track-item {

#cfm-drawer.cfm-mode-cco .cfm-track-item:hover,

.cfm-brand {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  min-width: 130px; flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-brand-logo {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; letter-spacing: 0.5px; white-space: nowrap;
}
.cfm-brand-logo span { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-on-air {
  font-size: 0.55rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 1.5px;
  text-transform: uppercase; color: #ef4444;
  background: rgba(239,68,68,0.12); border: 1px solid rgba(239,68,68,0.3);
  border-radius: 3px; padding: 0.1rem 0.35rem;
  animation: cfm-pulse 2s ease-in-out infinite;
  transition: color 0.3s, background 0.3s, border-color 0.3s;
}
.cfm-on-air.off-air {
  color: #445; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); border-color: rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  animation: none;
}
@keyframes cfm-pulse { 0%,100% { opacity:1; } 50% { opacity:0.5; } }

.cfm-song-info {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.75rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  min-width: 210px; max-width: 260px; flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-art {
  width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 6px; flex-shrink: 0;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  font-size: 1.2rem;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  transition: background 0.3s;
}
.cfm-meta { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-meta-title {
  font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 600; color: #e2e8f0;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-sub {
  font-size: 0.68rem; color: #556; margin-top: 0.1rem;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-genre {
  display: inline-block; font-size: 0.6rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff);
  background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border-radius: 3px;
  padding: 0.1rem 0.35rem; margin-top: 0.15rem; letter-spacing: 0.5px;
}
.cfm-heart {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1rem;
  color: #445; transition: color 0.2s, transform 0.15s; flex-shrink: 0; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-heart.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-heart:hover { transform: scale(1.2); }

.cfm-controls {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1.25rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0.4rem;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: color 0.18s, background 0.18s, transform 0.15s;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  width: 30px; height: 30px;
}
.cfm-btn:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn {
  width: 38px; height: 38px; font-size: 1rem;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); color: #040d1f;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: all 0.18s;
}
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn:hover { transform: scale(1.08); filter: brightness(1.15); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-active { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }

.cfm-progress-zone {
  flex: 1; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.6rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; min-width: 0;
}
.cfm-time { font-size: 0.68rem; color: #445; flex-shrink: 0; min-width: 32px; }
.cfm-time.right { text-align: right; }
.cfm-bar-wrap { flex: 1; position: relative; height: 4px; cursor: pointer; }
.cfm-bar-bg {
  position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
}
.cfm-bar-fill {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; bottom: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); width: 0%; transition: width 0.1s linear;
}
.cfm-bar-thumb {
  position: absolute; top: 50%; width: 12px; height: 12px;
  border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
  opacity: 0; transition: opacity 0.18s; box-shadow: 0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.4);
  left: 0%;
}
.cfm-bar-wrap:hover .cfm-bar-thumb { opacity: 1; }

.cfm-volume-zone {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1rem; border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-vol-icon { font-size: 0.75rem; color: #445; cursor: pointer; }
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider {
  -webkit-appearance: none; appearance: none;
  width: 70px; height: 3px; border-radius: 3px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); outline: none; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-webkit-slider-thumb {
  -webkit-appearance: none; width: 16px; height: 16px; border-radius: 50%;
  background: #fff; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-moz-range-thumb {
  width: 12px; height: 12px; border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; cursor: pointer; border: none;
}

.cfm-playlist-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0 1rem;
  transition: color 0.18s; flex-shrink: 0; height: 100%;
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.35rem; font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-playlist-btn:hover { color: #fff; }
.cfm-playlist-btn.open { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-playlist-text { font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; }
.cfm-playlist-count {
  display: inline-grid; place-items: center;
  min-width: 1.35rem; height: 1.35rem; padding: 0 0.28rem;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 800;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle {
  position: relative;
  height: 100%;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  padding: 0 0.85rem;
  border: none;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  background: rgba(217,154,49,0.04);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  flex-shrink: 0;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle span {
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.28);
  border-radius: 999px;
  padding: 0.22rem 0.52rem;
  color: #d99a31;
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 900;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover span,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible span,
.cfm-cco-toggle.active span {
  color: #080905;
  background: #d99a31;
  border-color: #d99a31;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after {
  content: attr(data-tip);
  position: absolute;
  right: 0.5rem;
  bottom: calc(100% + 10px);
  width: min(300px, calc(100vw - 24px));
  padding: 0.65rem 0.75rem;
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.34);
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: rgba(6,3,16,0.96);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  box-shadow: 0 14px 34px rgba(0,0,0,0.42);
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 650;
  line-height: 1.45;
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
  transform: translateY(4px);
  transition: opacity 0.16s ease, transform 0.16s ease;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover::after,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible::after {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle::after {
  content: none !important;
  display: none !important;
}

/* Playlist drawer */
#cfm-drawer {
  position: fixed; bottom: 68px; right: 0;
  width: 380px; max-height: min(560px, calc(100vh - 92px));
  background: #080414;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  border-radius: 14px 0 0 0;
  overflow-y: auto; z-index: 9998;
  display: none;
  box-shadow: -4px -4px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.5);
}
#cfm-drawer.open { display: block; }
.cfm-drawer-hdr {
  position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 1;
  padding: 0.85rem 1rem 0.75rem;
  background: #080414;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-drawer-title-row {
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 0.75rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-title {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.2px;
}
.cfm-drawer-count { color: #556; font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; white-space: nowrap; }
.cfm-drawer-actions {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.45rem; margin-top: 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  padding: 0.35rem 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.active { color: #ef4444; border-color: rgba(239,68,68,0.34); background: rgba(239,68,68,0.08); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.disabled { opacity: 0.45; cursor: default; }
.cfm-drawer-empty {
  padding: 1rem;
  color: #8a9bb0;
  font-size: 0.82rem;
  line-height: 1.55;
}
.cfm-track-item {
  display: grid; grid-template-columns: 22px minmax(0, 1fr) auto auto; align-items: center; gap: 0.65rem;
  padding: 0.65rem 1rem; cursor: pointer;
  background: #080414;
  transition: background 0.15s; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.04);
}
.cfm-track-item:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); }
.cfm-track-item.active { background: #11172d; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped { opacity: 0.58; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped .cfm-track-name { text-decoration: line-through; }
.cfm-track-marker {
  display: grid; place-items: center;
  width: 22px; min-width: 22px;
}
.cfm-track-num {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.8rem; color: #334;
  min-width: 18px; text-align: center;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-num { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-track-dot {
  width: 8px; height: 8px; border-radius: 50%;
  animation: cfm-pulse 1s ease-in-out infinite; flex-shrink: 0;
  display: none;
}
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-dot { display: block; }
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-num { display: none; }
.cfm-track-info { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-track-name {
  font-size: 0.82rem; font-weight: 600; color: #c0cdd8;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-name { color: #fff; }
.cfm-track-genre { font-size: 0.67rem; color: #445; margin-top: 0.1rem; }
.cfm-track-fav {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #334; transition: color 0.18s; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-track-fav.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-track-skip {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #66758a;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.64rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1;
  padding: 0.32rem 0.48rem;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.cfm-track-skip:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
.cfm-track-skip.active { color: #f59e0b; border-color: rgba(245,158,11,0.34); background: rgba(245,158,11,0.08); }

/* Scrollbar styling for drawer */
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar { width: 4px; }
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar-track { background: transparent; }
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); border-radius: 2px; }

/* Body padding to account for player */
body.has-cfm-player { padding-bottom: 68px; }

/* ── Homepage sidebar player ── */

  background: linear-gradient(160deg, #0a0e20 0%, #060912 100%);
  border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.28);
  border-top: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.5);
  border-radius: 14px;
  overflow: hidden;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  box-shadow: 0 4px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.5), inset 0 1px 0 rgba(74,158,255,0.08);
}
.cfm-sb-header {
  padding: 0.7rem 0.85rem;
  background: rgba(74,158,255,0.08);
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.12);
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between;
  gap: 0.55rem;
}
.cfm-sb-name {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.05rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; letter-spacing: 0.5px; white-space: nowrap;
}
.cfm-sb-name span { color: #4a9eff; }
.cfm-sb-header-actions {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.35rem; flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-sb-list-btn {
  border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.26);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(74,158,255,0.08);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1;
  padding: 0.32rem 0.42rem;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  gap: 0.24rem;
  transition: color 0.18s, background 0.18s, border-color 0.18s;
}
.cfm-sb-list-btn:hover,
.cfm-sb-list-btn.open {
  color: #fff;

}
.cfm-sb-list-count {
  display: inline-grid;
  place-items: center;
  min-width: 1.3rem;
  height: 1.3rem;
  padding: 0 0.25rem;
  border-radius: 999px;

  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 900;
}
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle {
  position: relative;
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.28);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(217,154,49,0.06);
  color: #d99a31;
  cursor: pointer;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 900;
  line-height: 1;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
  padding: 0.43rem 0.56rem;
}
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle:hover,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle:focus-visible,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle.active {
  color: #080905;
  background: #d99a31;
  border-color: #d99a31;
}
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle::after {
  content: attr(data-tip);
  position: absolute;
  right: 0;
  top: calc(100% + 10px);
  width: min(280px, calc(100vw - 32px));

  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.34);
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: rgba(6,3,16,0.96);
  color: #dbe8f7;

  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 650;
  letter-spacing: 0;

  opacity: 0;

.cfm-sb-cco-toggle:hover::after,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle:focus-visible::after {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle::after {
  content: none !important;
  display: none !important;
}
.cfm-sb-art-wrap {
  width: 100%; padding-top: 62%; position: relative;
  background:
    linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(10,30,50,0.85), rgba(12,21,43,0.78)),
    radial-gradient(circle at center, rgba(86,167,255,0.1), transparent 60%);
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.14);
  overflow: hidden;
}
.cfm-sb-art {
  position: absolute; inset: 0;
  display: block;
  transition: box-shadow 0.4s;
}
.cfm-sb-art.playing {
  animation: cfm-sb-glow 3s ease-in-out infinite;
}
.cfm-sb-art-grid {
  position: absolute; inset: 0;
  background:
    linear-gradient(rgba(146,181,255,0.06) 1px, transparent 1px),
    linear-gradient(90deg, rgba(146,181,255,0.06) 1px, transparent 1px);
  background-size: 20px 20px;
  -webkit-mask-image: radial-gradient(circle at center, black 22%, transparent 78%);
          mask-image: radial-gradient(circle at center, black 22%, transparent 78%);

.cfm-sb-art-arc {
  position: absolute; left: 50%; top: 50%;
  border: 1px solid rgba(115,151,237,0.18);
  border-radius: 50%;
  transform: translate(-50%, -50%);

      <span class="sa-headline-tag">The Short Version</span>
      <h2>Your set-aside status determines what you can compete for. Your size status determines whether your set-aside status is even real.</h2>
      <p>Most new contractors learn the alphabet soup (8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, SDVOSB) and stop there. The harder questions are: What does each category actually qualify you for? When does the CO have to use them? How does SBA decide if you're "small" in the first place? And what happens when your business grows past the size threshold during a contract you already won?</p>
      <p>This page covers all of it from the contracting officer's chair, with the specific SBA regulations you can verify against. <strong>Get this right and you compete for the right work. Get it wrong and you lose contracts to size protests, debarment, or worse.</strong></p>

    <!-- WHAT SET-ASIDES ARE -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="what-set-asides-are">
      <h2>What set-asides actually are (and why they exist)</h2>

      <p>A <strong>small business set-aside</strong> is a federal acquisition that's restricted so only small businesses (or a specific category of small business) can compete. Large businesses cannot bid on a set-aside acquisition, full stop. The legal authority is the <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/644" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Small Business Act, 15 U.S.C. § 644</a>, with SBA's program rules at <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-125" target="_blank" rel="noopener">13 CFR Part 125</a> and the related certification program parts.</p>

      <p>The reason set-asides exist is that Congress established statutory goals for the federal government to award a minimum percentage of prime contract dollars to small businesses each year. The current government-wide goal is <strong>23% to small business</strong>, with sub-goals including 5% to women-owned small businesses, 5% to small disadvantaged businesses (including 8(a)), 3% to HUBZone small businesses, and 5% to service-disabled veteran-owned small businesses. The Small Business Administration (SBA) tracks performance against these goals annually.</p>

      <p>Set-asides are the primary tool COs use to hit those goals. When a CO sets aside an acquisition, they're saying: "for this contract, only small businesses (or only 8(a) firms, or only HUBZone firms, etc.) get to bid." Large businesses are out.</p>

      <p>A few things to know up front:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Set-asides are not optional.</strong> The Rule of Two (covered below) requires COs to set aside acquisitions when the conditions are met. The CO does not get to decide based on convenience.</li>
        <li><strong>Set-asides are not limited to small dollar values.</strong> Multi-million dollar contracts get set aside all the time when the CO finds qualified small business sources.</li>
        <li><strong>Set-aside eligibility is not the same as award.</strong> You still have to bid, propose, and win. The set-aside just controls who's allowed to compete.</li>
      </ul>
    </div>

    <!-- THE TYPES -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="types">
      <h2>The set-aside types, in plain English</h2>

      <p>There are several flavors of set-aside. Each has its own eligibility rules, its own certification requirements, and its own typical use cases. Here's the practical breakdown:</p>

      <table class="sa-table">
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Set-Aside Type</th><th>Who Qualifies</th><th>Certification Path</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Total Small Business Set-Aside</strong></td>
            <td>Any small business under the relevant NAICS size standard.</td>
            <td>No formal SBA certification required. Self-representation in SAM, verified at award time.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>8(a) Business Development</strong></td>
            <td>Small businesses owned and controlled at least 51% by socially and economically disadvantaged US citizens. Nine-year program with substantial set-aside and sole-source authority.</td>
            <td><strong>SBA-certified.</strong> Application takes months. <a href="https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-assistance-programs/8a-business-development-program" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA 8(a) program</a>.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>HUBZone</strong></td>
            <td>Small businesses with a principal office located in a HUBZone (Historically Underutilized Business Zone) and at least 35% of employees living in HUBZones.</td>
            <td><strong>SBA-certified.</strong> Recertification is generally required every three years; the business must keep meeting program requirements and report applicable material changes. <a href="https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-assistance-programs/hubzone-program" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA HUBZone program</a>.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>WOSB / EDWOSB</strong></td>
            <td>Women-Owned Small Business / Economically Disadvantaged Women-Owned Small Business. At least 51% owned and controlled by one or more women who are US citizens.</td>
            <td><strong>SBA-certified</strong> (self-cert no longer accepted for set-asides since 2020). <a href="https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-assistance-programs/women-owned-small-business-federal-contracting-program" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA WOSB program</a>.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>SDVOSB and VOSB</strong></td>
            <td>Service-Disabled Veteran-Owned Small Business / Veteran-Owned Small Business. At least 51% owned by one or more service-disabled or veteran owners who actively manage the business.</td>
            <td><strong>SBA VetCert-certified.</strong> Certified SDVOSBs can compete for federal-wide SDVOSB set-asides and sole-source awards. VOSB-specific set-aside and sole-source authority is principally associated with the VA's Vets First program. <a href="https://www.sba.gov/federal-contracting/contracting-assistance-programs/veteran-contracting-assistance-programs" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA veteran contracting programs</a>.</td>
          </tr>
          <tr>
            <td><strong>Small Disadvantaged Business (SDB)</strong></td>
            <td>Small business at least 51% owned by socially and economically disadvantaged individuals. Used for representation and reporting purposes.</td>
            <td>Self-certified for representation. Does NOT by itself qualify you for an 8(a) set-aside; that requires formal SBA 8(a) certification.</td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <h3>Partial set-asides and reserves</h3>
      <p>Two related mechanisms worth knowing:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Partial set-asides</strong> split a single acquisition into a set-aside portion and an unrestricted portion. Used when the CO can identify a portion of the work appropriate for small business but cannot reasonably set aside the entire acquisition.</li>
        <li><strong>Reserves</strong> apply to multiple-award contracts. A reserve sets aside one or more awards under a multiple-award solicitation for small businesses, even when the overall solicitation is unrestricted.</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="warn-box">
        <strong>The "ineligible for one program does not mean ineligible for all" point.</strong> A small business can hold multiple eligible certifications at once (e.g., a small business can be both HUBZone and WOSB). Your eligibility for any one set-aside is independent of your eligibility for the others.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- PROGRAM SELECTION -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="order-of-preference">
      <h2>How COs choose among set-aside programs</h2>

      <p>There is no general order of precedence among the 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB, and WOSB programs. Above the SAT, the CO considers those socioeconomic programs before using a total small business set-aside, but does not work through a universal ranked list of the four programs.</p>

      <p>The choice among programs is based on:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Market research and capable sources</strong> in each eligible program</li>
        <li><strong>Agency progress toward its small business goals</strong></li>
        <li><strong>The applicable program rules</strong> for the requirement</li>
        <li><strong>8(a) follow-on status.</strong> A requirement already accepted into the 8(a) program generally remains there unless SBA agrees to release it.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>Sole-source authorities are separate tools with their own conditions and thresholds. They do not mean one socioeconomic program universally outranks another.</p>

      <div class="tip-box">
        <strong>What this means for you strategically.</strong> A valid 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB, or WOSB certification gives you access to competitions reserved for that program. It does not put you higher in a universal queue; the value of the certification depends on the requirement, capable-source market, agency goals, and program rules.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- SIZE STANDARDS -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="size-standards">
      <h2>Size standards: how SBA decides if you're "small"</h2>

      <p>Every NAICS code has a size standard published by SBA. These standards tell you the maximum size a business can be and still qualify as "small" under that NAICS. The full table lives at <a href="https://www.sba.gov/document/support-table-size-standards" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA's size standards table</a>.</p>

      <h3>Two flavors of size standard</h3>

      <p>SBA uses two main types of size standards:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Revenue-based</strong> (most service NAICS, agriculture, construction): your average annual receipts over the last <strong>5 fiscal years</strong> determine your size. The 5-year window changed from 3 years to 5 years per the SBA Runway Extension Act of 2018, which gave growing businesses more runway before they "graduate" to large.</li>
        <li><strong>Employee-based</strong> (most manufacturing, mining, some retail and IT): your average number of employees over the <strong>preceding completed 24 calendar months</strong> determines your size. Part-time and temporary employees count the same as full-time employees.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>A few examples to make this concrete:</p>

      <table class="sa-table">
        <thead>
          <tr><th>NAICS</th><th>Description</th><th>Size Standard</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td><code>541512</code></td><td>Computer Systems Design Services</td><td>$34M average annual receipts</td></tr>
          <tr><td><code>561720</code></td><td>Janitorial Services</td><td>$22M average annual receipts</td></tr>
          <tr><td><code>236220</code></td><td>Commercial & Institutional Construction</td><td>$45M average annual receipts</td></tr>
          <tr><td><code>332994</code></td><td>Small Arms, Ordnance, & Accessories Manufacturing</td><td>1,500 employees</td></tr>
          <tr><td><code>336411</code></td><td>Aircraft Manufacturing</td><td>1,500 employees</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>

      <p>(Numbers above are illustrative; check SBA's table for current values, which update periodically.)</p>

      <h3>Affiliation: the rule that wrecks size status</h3>

      <p>Your size includes the size of your <strong>affiliates</strong>. SBA's affiliation rules at <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-121/subpart-A/subject-group-ECFR45c34c40fd0664f/section-121.103" target="_blank" rel="noopener">13 CFR 121.103</a> determine when two entities should be treated as one for size purposes. Common affiliation triggers:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Common ownership or control</strong> (you and another company share the same owner or controlling shareholder)</li>
        <li><strong>Common management</strong> (same officers, directors, or controlling parties)</li>
        <li><strong>Identity of interest</strong> (family ties between owners of separate firms)</li>
        <li><strong>Newly organized concern</strong> rule (a new firm started by former employees of a related entity)</li>
        <li><strong>Ostensible subcontractor rule</strong> (when your "subcontractor" is doing the primary and vital work; covered in the <a href="subcontracting-trap.html">Subcontracting Trap guide</a>)</li>
        <li><strong>Joint venture affiliation</strong> (default rule unless you fit a specific exception like an SBA-approved mentor-protégé JV)</li>
      </ul>

      <p>Affiliation is fact-specific and SBA looks at the totality of circumstances. If you have any kind of corporate parent, sister company, significant investor, family-related business, or controlling outside party, talk to an attorney experienced in federal procurement before claiming small business status. APEX Accelerators can help you find one for free.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- HOW TO CHECK -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="check-status">
      <h2>How to check your size status</h2>

      <p>For each NAICS code that's relevant to your business, do this:</p>

      <ol>
        <li><strong>Find the size standard</strong> on <a href="https://www.sba.gov/document/support-table-size-standards" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA's size standards table</a>. Find your NAICS, note whether it's revenue-based or employee-based, and the threshold.</li>
        <li><strong>Calculate your number</strong> using your actual records. For receipts-based standards: average annual receipts over the five most recently completed fiscal years. For employee-based standards: average the number of employees over the preceding completed 24 calendar months; part-time and temporary employees count the same as full-time employees.</li>
        <li><strong>Add affiliates if any apply.</strong> Use the affiliation rules at 13 CFR 121.103. If unsure, get legal advice before claiming small status.</li>
        <li><strong>Compare to the threshold.</strong> If your number is at or below the threshold, you qualify as small under that NAICS. Above, you do not.</li>
        <li><strong>Update your SAM record</strong> to reflect your size status by NAICS. SAM will calculate this for you when you complete or update your registration, but the underlying inputs (your reported receipts, headcount, and ownership/affiliation answers) have to be accurate.</li>
      </ol>

      <p>You can be small under one NAICS and large under another. Your SAM record reflects your size by NAICS, and contracting officers check your status under the specific NAICS they used for the solicitation.</p>

      <div class="tip-box">
        <strong>SBA also provides a free online "Size Standards Tool"</strong> at <a href="https://www.sba.gov/size-standards/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">sba.gov/size-standards</a>. You enter your NAICS, your revenue or headcount, and it tells you whether you qualify as small. Use it as a sanity check, not as legal advice.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- RECERTIFICATION -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="recertification">
      <h2>Recertification and the "size at time of offer" rule</h2>

      <p>Size status is not a one-time determination. SBA requires you to recertify your size in several specific situations.</p>

      <h3>Size at time of offer</h3>
      <p>The general rule from <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-121/subpart-A/subject-group-ECFR8d76d2cf94d68ed/section-121.404" target="_blank" rel="noopener">13 CFR 121.404</a> is that your size is determined as of <strong>the date of your initial offer</strong> on a contract. If you certified small at offer time and you grow large during performance, you generally remain small for the original contract. That's the protection that lets growing small businesses keep their existing awards.</p>

      <p>But there are several exceptions where you have to recertify, and your status might change:</p>

      <h3>When recertification is required</h3>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>End of the fifth year of long-term contracts.</strong> If you're on a contract longer than five years (including options), SBA requires recertification at the five-year mark and again before each subsequent option exercise. If you're large at recertification, the agency cannot count future task orders or option exercises toward small business goals.</li>
        <li><strong>Before exercising any option that extends the period of performance more than five years past contract award.</strong></li>
        <li><strong>After a merger, acquisition, sale, or change in ownership.</strong> SBA wants to know within 30 days whether the deal changes your size status. The acquiring firm's size is now part of the calculation.</li>
        <li><strong>Annually in your SAM record.</strong> Reps and certs (which include your size representation) require update at least once per year as part of keeping your SAM registration active.</li>
        <li><strong>Before each new offer.</strong> Each time you submit a proposal, you're certifying your size status as of that date.</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>What "growing out of small" actually means</h3>
      <p>If your average revenue or headcount crosses the size threshold for your primary NAICS, you've "grown out of small" under that NAICS. You don't lose your existing contracts, but you become ineligible for future small business set-aside awards under that NAICS until either (a) you fall back below the threshold or (b) the threshold goes up. You can still win <em>unrestricted</em> awards as a large business, and you can still be small under other NAICS codes if your size is below those thresholds.</p>

      <div class="warn-box">
        <strong>Don't keep claiming small after you've grown out of it.</strong> Continuing to bid on small business set-asides after you cross the size threshold can jeopardize an award and, when the required legal elements are present, create civil or criminal liability. Competitors can and do file size protests at SBA when they see a vendor they believe has grown beyond their threshold. <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-13/chapter-I/part-121/subpart-A/subject-group-ECFR2d3d1ad7ada1f60/section-121.1004" target="_blank" rel="noopener">SBA's size protest procedures</a> are public and well-used.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- RULE OF TWO -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="rule-of-two">
      <h2>The Rule of Two</h2>

      <p>The Rule of Two is the engine that drives most small business set-aside volume. The rule reads, in plain language:</p>

      <p>The contracting officer <strong>shall</strong> set aside any acquisition over the simplified acquisition threshold for small business participation when there is a reasonable expectation that:</p>
      <ol>
        <li>Offers will be obtained from at least <strong>two responsible small business concerns</strong> offering the products of different small business concerns; AND</li>
        <li>Award will be made at <strong>fair market prices</strong>.</li>
      </ol>

      <p>The word "shall" is doing the work in that sentence. If both conditions are met, the CO is <em>required</em> to set aside the acquisition. It's not optional. It's not a preference. The CO can't decide it's easier to compete unrestricted.</p>

      <h3>How COs apply the Rule of Two</h3>
      <p>Before a CO can set aside an acquisition, they have to do market research demonstrating both prongs:</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>"Two responsible small business concerns."</strong> The CO looks at SAM, prior award history (USAspending.gov, FPDS), capability statements submitted by industry, sources sought responses, and informal industry days. They need to find at least two specific small businesses that look capable and responsible.</li>
        <li><strong>"Fair market prices."</strong> The CO uses prior contract data, GSA schedule pricing, commercial market research, and IGCEs to confirm the small business segment can deliver at reasonable prices.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>If you want your business considered in a CO's Rule of Two analysis, the most direct path is to <strong>respond to sources sought notices</strong> on SAM.gov. A sources sought notice is the CO formally asking industry "who can do this?" When you respond with a capability statement, you've added yourself to the CO's list of identified small business sources for that requirement.</p>

      <h3>The Rule of Two for tier-specific set-asides</h3>
      <p>The Rule of Two also applies to program-specific set-asides. If a CO has a reasonable expectation of receiving offers from at least two responsible HUBZone firms (or 8(a), WOSB/EDWOSB, or SDVOSB firms), they can set aside the acquisition for that specific category, subject to the applicable program rules.</p>

      <div class="co-voice">
        <span class="co-tag">From the CO's chair</span>
        <p><strong>If you see an RFI or sources sought notice on SAM, please get involved.</strong> Most contractors think these notices are just "fishing" by the CO. They're not. They're how I do the actual Rule of Two analysis that determines whether the eventual solicitation goes out as set aside, and to whom.</p>
        <p>Here's an example. I'm scoping a services acquisition I think will go around $5M. I post a sources sought looking for capable small businesses. I get 30 responses. Twelve of them are SDVOSBs. Now I have a real decision: do I set aside as a total small business set-aside (all 30 in the pool) or set aside specifically for SDVOSB (12 in the pool)? <strong>If the SDVOSB pool is large enough to expect competition and reasonable pricing, I'd much rather set aside SDVOSB.</strong> Smaller pool to evaluate. Helps the agency's SDVOSB goal. Same fair-market-prices outcome.</p>
        <p>If you're an SDVOSB and you didn't respond, you weren't in that count. The set-aside decision is shaped by who showed up. If only 3 SDVOSBs responded instead of 12, I would not have set aside SDVOSB-only because the competition pool would be too thin. Your response (or absence) directly shapes the competition you'll face.</p>
        <p>Same logic applies to HUBZone, WOSB, and 8(a). If you're in any specific socio-economic category, responding to sources sought is how you tell me "use your authority to set this aside in a way that benefits me." If you don't speak up, I work with what I have.</p>
        <p><strong>One more thing the RFI is good for: pushing back on the NAICS.</strong> If a different NAICS better fits the work, the RFI is your chance to make that case. Tell me which NAICS best describes the principal purpose and why, using the industry descriptions, the function of the supplies or services, and the relative value and importance of the requirement's components. Do not base the argument on which size standard produces the preferred competition pool. I may or may not use it. Sometimes I picked the NAICS because it's the one my customer used last time and I never thought about it again. A well-reasoned RFI response that says "this looks more like NAICS X than NAICS Y, here's why" can change the solicitation. The worst case is I disagree and stick with my pick. There's no downside to making the case.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- WHAT COS CHECK -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="what-cos-check">
      <h2>What COs check during market research</h2>

      <p>Before a CO sets aside an acquisition, and again before award, they verify your status. Here's what runs through their head:</p>

      <div class="co-voice">
        <span class="co-tag">From the CO's chair</span>
        <p><strong>Market research stage.</strong> I'm running a sources sought or just doing the homework before drafting the solicitation. I open SAM and search by NAICS to see what small businesses are registered. I check capability statements I've collected. I look at USAspending and FPDS to see who's won similar work in the past. I cross-reference SBA's databases for 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, and SDVOSB certifications. If I can identify two or more responsible small businesses (in the applicable program, at the right capability level, willing to bid), I set aside the acquisition. <strong>If you didn't put yourself in front of me, you weren't in this analysis.</strong></p>

        <p><strong>Pre-award verification.</strong> Once I've got a winning offeror, before I sign anything, I re-verify everything: SAM registration is active, size status is current under the NAICS I solicited, certifications (8(a)/HUBZone/WOSB/SDVOSB) are still valid in SBA's databases, no exclusions or debarment flags. If any of these don't check out, I have to pull the award and re-evaluate.</p>

        <p><strong>If a competitor protests.</strong> Size protests are common after award. SBA's Office of Government Contracting investigates. The losing offeror sometimes files. Larger competitors looking for a way to disqualify a winning small business sometimes file. If a protest comes in, your size and certification record gets a much closer look. If you misrepresented anything, this is when it surfaces.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- PITFALLS -->
    <div class="sa-section" id="pitfalls">
      <h2>The pitfalls that cost vendors awards</h2>

      <ol>
        <li><strong>Self-certifying as 8(a), HUBZone, WOSB, or SDVOSB without SBA certification.</strong> All four require formal SBA certification for program set-aside award eligibility. An unsupported representation does not establish eligibility and can trigger serious penalties when knowingly false. SBA verifies against its own databases at award.</li>

        <li><strong>Stale size status.</strong> Your business has grown over the threshold and you haven't updated your SAM record. You're claiming small on bids you're no longer eligible for.</li>

        <li><strong>Misunderstanding the "size at time of offer" rule.</strong> Some contractors think they can never lose small business eligibility once they win a contract. Wrong. Long-term contracts trigger recertification at year five and at each option, and mergers/acquisitions trigger immediate recertification.</li>

        <li><strong>Picking the wrong NAICS code on your offer.</strong> If you bid as small under a NAICS where you're actually large (because you picked one with a higher size threshold than the one the solicitation used), the award gets pulled.</li>

        <li><strong>Affiliation you didn't think mattered.</strong> Your spouse's business, your former employer where you still consult, your investor who has board control. SBA's affiliation rules can sweep in entities you wouldn't intuitively combine. Get advice before claiming small status if you have any of these.</li>

        <li><strong>HUBZone employees moving.</strong> HUBZone certification requires that 35% of your employees live in HUBZones. If your workforce moves and you fall below 35%, you lose HUBZone status. Some firms hire intentionally to maintain the threshold. Others lose certification because they didn't track it.</li>

        <li><strong>Letting your 8(a) program participation lapse.</strong> 8(a) is a nine-year program with annual reviews. Failure to comply with program requirements (annual financial reporting, business plan updates, mentor-protégé reporting) can get you suspended or terminated from the program early.</li>

        <li><strong>Ignoring the recertification deadline on long-term contracts.</strong> If you're on a five-year contract and SBA requires recertification at year five, and you don't recertify, the agency loses the ability to count future option exercises toward small business goals. Some COs will not exercise the option as a result.</li>

        <li><strong>Not responding to sources sought.</strong> The Rule of Two only protects you if the CO knew about you. Skipping sources sought because you "don't want to give away your strategy" is a way to ensure no set-asides go your way.</li>

        <li><strong>Treating set-aside status as a substitute for capability.</strong> Set-aside eligibility lets you compete. It doesn't get you awarded. You still have to put together a real proposal, demonstrate real capability, and have real past performance. The contractors who treat the small business cert as a free pass are the ones who get out-competed by other small businesses with actual specialization.</li>
      </ol>
    </div>

    <!-- CTA -->
    <div class="cta-box">
      <h3>Got the size status right? Now make sure your reps and certs match.</h3>
      <p>Your size status, socio-economic certifications, and integrity disclosures all live in your SAM reps and certs. The CO reads them before reading your proposal. The <a href="sam-reps-and-certs.html" style="color:#fff;text-decoration:underline;">SAM Reps and Certs guide</a> walks through the categories from a CO's perspective.</p>

    .article-bg { background: #040d1f; padding: 3rem 1.5rem 6rem; }

    .breadcrumb a { color: var(--accent); text-decoration: none; font-weight: 600; }
    .breadcrumb a:hover { text-decoration: underline; }
    .breadcrumb-sep { margin: 0 .45rem; color: #475569; }
    .breadcrumb-current { color: var(--silver); }

      font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif;
      font-size: 1.6rem; font-weight: 700;
      color: var(--white);

      line-height: 1.25;
      letter-spacing: .2px;

      display: inline-block;
      font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
      font-size: .7rem; font-weight: 700;
      letter-spacing: 1.5px; text-transform: uppercase;

      border-radius: 4px;
      margin-left: .6rem;

@keyframes cfm-sb-glow { 0%,100% { box-shadow: inset 0 0 40px rgba(74,158,255,0.07); } 50% { box-shadow: inset 0 0 80px rgba(74,158,255,0.14); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-eq { 0%,100% { transform: scaleY(0.6); } 50% { transform: scaleY(1.12); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-spin { from { transform: rotate(0deg); } to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-orbit-a {
  0%   { transform: translate(0, 0); }
  25%  { transform: translate(14px, 8px); }
  50%  { transform: translate(32px, 26px); }
  75%  { transform: translate(10px, 46px); }
  100% { transform: translate(0, 0); }
}
@keyframes cfm-sb-orbit-b {
  0%   { transform: translate(0, 0); }
  25%  { transform: translate(-12px, -8px); }
  50%  { transform: translate(-28px, -22px); }
  75%  { transform: translate(-8px, -42px); }
  100% { transform: translate(0, 0); }
}

    <span class="hero-badge">The Big Question</span>
    <h1 class="page-hero-title">AI Use in Acquisitions</h1>
    <p class="page-hero-sub">Where it earns its keep. Where it is overhyped. Where the approved-tool mandate is making federal contracting worse instead of better.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="article-bg">
  <div class="article-wrap">

    <div class="breadcrumb">
      <a href="index.html">Home</a>
      <span class="breadcrumb-sep">/</span>
      <a href="ai-acquisitions.html">AI in Acquisitions</a>
      <span class="breadcrumb-sep">/</span>
      <span class="breadcrumb-current">AI Use in Acquisitions</span>
    </div>

    <div class="article">

      <p>The rest of this track covers the tools, how I build with them, and the short list of places they do not belong. This page is where I put a stake in the ground on the question I get asked most: how much of this should we actually be using?</p>

      <p>Short answer: more than most contracting offices are using it now, in a specific set of places, with a clear sense of where it should not go. The long answer is the next few sections.</p>

      <h2>Where it earns its keep <span class="h2-tag yes">Yes</span></h2>

      <p>Every one of these is something I do in a normal week, on unclassified and non-proprietary material, with the best commercial tool I can get my hands on.</p>

      <h3>Cleaning up the prose you were already going to write</h3>
      <p>Email drafts, memos for record, PNM entries, customer updates, the opening paragraph of a market research report, the cover email for a package you are routing. Text in, text out. No data you do not already own leaves your head. This is the high-frequency, low-drama use case, and it is the bulk of the value for most COs.</p>

      <h3>Explaining something you have not had to explain before</h3>
      <p>Paste in a FAR part you have not touched in two years and ask for the plain-English read. Walk through a clause with a program manager who just rotated in. Prep for a warrant-board oral by having the model role-play a panel member. Frontier models are remarkable at this when you give them the source material and ask clean questions. It is the closest thing to a patient, always-available, infinitely-recallable study partner that has ever existed.</p>

      <h3>Getting past the blank page</h3>
      <p>Synopsis skeletons, PWS outlines, a rough first draft of a D&F for a buy you have not written before. You were going to edit the thing into the ground anyway. Let AI get you to a bad first draft in five minutes so you can spend the rest of the hour making it right. Starting is the expensive step.</p>

      <h3>Building tools for yourself</h3>
      <p>Covered at length on <a href="ai-building.html">Building Tools with AI</a>. Excel workbooks with the right formulas baked in, scoring templates, IGCE roll-ups, mini dashboards. AI builds the thing. You run it on your own machine with the real numbers. None of the data ever crosses the chat window.</p>

      <h3>Studying</h3>
      <p>Quiz me on Part 19. Explain every exception to full and open competition. Walk me through how a CPARS rating gets challenged. Simulate a source-selection dispute and make me defend the position. This is where I have personally gotten the most out of AI during board prep, and it is a use case almost nobody talks about because it is quiet and individual.</p>

      <h3>Translating acquisition into customer-speak</h3>
      <p>Take a paragraph of FAR or DFARS language and rewrite it for a program office, an operational commander, a resource advisor, or a customer who does not live in this world. The workforce that can do that translation well is the workforce customers want to work with. AI makes that translation cheap, which makes you faster and more responsive.</p>

      <div class="yes-box">
        <span class="yes-title">The shape</span>
        <p><strong>Text you own going in, text you will edit going out.</strong> That is the sweet spot. Everything in this section fits that pattern. Nothing sensitive is riding along, and your judgment is the final filter on the way out.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pull-quote">
        The honest answer is that most COs should be using AI more than they are, in specific places, with a clear sense of where it should not go.
      </div>

      <h2>Where it is overhyped <span class="h2-tag hype">Hype</span></h2>

      <p>These are the pitches that sound good in a conference keynote and fall apart on contact with the job.</p>

      <h3>"AI will evaluate proposals for us"</h3>
      <p>It will not, and it should not, at least not without explicit disclosure to offerors up front. The full argument is on <a href="ai-not-using.html">When NOT to Use AI</a>. The short version: source selection is a defensible-judgment exercise, and "the model said so" is not a rationale that survives a GAO protest or a CO's own review of the record.</p>

      <h3>"AI will write my D&F for me"</h3>
      <p>The D&F is the written record of your judgment, and the signature on it is the decision. Let AI help with structure and language. Do not let it originate the reasoning. If a reviewer reads your D&F and hears a chatbot's voice, they are going to ask who was actually deciding. That is not a conversation you want to have.</p>

      <h3>"AI will do my market research"</h3>
      <p>A prompt like "do market research for X" gets you a confident-sounding collage of plausible nonsense. AI is excellent when you hand it public information you have already gathered and ask it to summarize, compare, or pull patterns. It is a liability when you ask it to invent the data on top of everything else. Hand it the raw material. Let it shape the output.</p>

      <h3>Citing regulation from memory</h3>
      <p>Models hallucinate FAR clause numbers, DFARS paragraph letters, and case names with a straight face. If a model cites a reg, pull the reg and verify. If the citation does not resolve, the citation does not exist. This is not a future-model problem. This is a today problem on every tool on the market.</p>

      <h3>"AI will replace contracting"</h3>
      <p>It will not. The signature is the decision, and the decision is the job. AI can carry a lot of the writing, a lot of the editing, a lot of the explaining. It cannot carry the warrant. The contracting shop shrinks where AI handles the repetitive work; it does not vanish.</p>

      <h2>Where "use the approved tool" is making things worse <span class="h2-tag policy">Policy</span></h2>

      <p>This is the part of the conversation the federal AI space does not want to have out loud, and it is the one I think matters most.</p>

      <p>The pattern: an agency or service stands up an approved AI tool. Sometimes it is a chat wrapper in front of a weaker foundation model. Sometimes it is a branded portal running a capability floor from a year or two ago. The workforce gets a policy that reads as "use this, do not use anything else." Meanwhile the frontier models are a browser tab away, an order of magnitude better for the unclassified, non-proprietary work that makes up most of a CO's day.</p>

      <p>A few things happen when the approved-tool mandate is that wide:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>COs try the approved tool on a real task and it falls over.</strong> They conclude AI is not worth the effort, because the only AI they have tried is the weakest one on the market.</li>
        <li><strong>The policy was written to govern data and reads like it governs models.</strong> Those are different problems. Data-class rules should be airtight. Model-choice rules, for public and self-owned text, should be wide open.</li>
        <li><strong>The approved tool gets frozen to a deployment snapshot</strong> while the commercial frontier advances every quarter. The gap grows. Nobody inside the mandate sees the gap because they are inside the mandate.</li>
        <li><strong>Workarounds multiply.</strong> People who need the better tool go find it on their personal device at home, or they do not use AI at all, or, worst case, they reach for the best tool on a work machine with data that should not be there. The mandate that was supposed to protect the edge case ends up shaping all the behavior around it.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>The security problem this mandate is trying to solve is real. ATO, authorized use policies, FedRAMP, contract vehicles, the specific conditions under which a model can legally see a given class of data: none of that is negotiable, and none of it is fake. The people standing up the approved tools are not doing it out of ignorance. They are doing it because somebody has to.</p>

      <p>The ask is not to throw those rules out. It is to evolve the policy from "use this specific model for everything" to "use the best tool available for the class of data in front of you." For unclassified, non-proprietary, non-SSS work (which, again, is most of the job), letting the workforce use the best tool on the market makes contracting faster, more accurate, and more responsive. Mandating the weakest tool does the opposite, and the workforce already knows it.</p>

      <div class="policy-box">
        <span class="policy-title">What good policy looks like</span>
        <p><strong>Govern the data, not the model.</strong> Keep the hard rules around proprietary, CUI, SSS, classified, PII, and privileged material. Stop pretending a mandated internal portal with a year-old capability floor is the right answer for everything outside those rings. The workforce is ready to use better tools responsibly. The policy has to let them.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="pull-quote">
        We do not need more approved tools. We need better ones, and we need to be honest about what the current approved ones can and cannot do.
      </div>

      <h2>A working rule of thumb</h2>

      <p>If I had to compress all of this into something you could repeat in a meeting:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Public data or your own words?</strong> Use the best tool you can get to.</li>
        <li><strong>Marked or sensitive?</strong> See <a href="ai-not-using.html">When NOT to Use AI</a>. The list is short, serious, and non-negotiable.</li>
        <li><strong>Deciding, not drafting?</strong> AI helps you think. You decide. The signature is yours.</li>
        <li><strong>Model cites a reg?</strong> Look up the reg. Every time.</li>
        <li><strong>Approved tool is the weaker choice for unclassified work?</strong> Push your shop on that. The workforce is better off when policy catches up to reality, and the conversation does not move unless COs have it.</li>
      </ul>

      <h2>The honest closing</h2>

      <p>AI is not going to fix federal contracting by itself, and it is not going to take anybody's job in the next five years. What it will do, for the COs who lean into it, is hand back hours every week, make your writing tighter, make your customer interactions better, and make your study habits sharper. That is a substantial unlock for the workforce that uses it well.</p>

      <p>The workforce that does not use it, because the only version they have been handed is the weak one, is getting left behind. That is a policy problem, and it is fixable. The first step is talking about it honestly.</p>

      <div class="checklist-box">
        <h3>TL;DR</h3>
        <ul>
          <li><strong>Use AI liberally on unclassified, non-proprietary text work.</strong> Email, memos, explanations, drafts, study prep, customer translation. That is the 60 percent.</li>
          <li><strong>Build tools with AI, don't feed it your data.</strong> Covered on <a href="ai-building.html">Building Tools with AI</a>.</li>
          <li><strong>Do not let AI originate the reasoning on a D&F.</strong> It can help with language. It cannot do the deciding.</li>
          <li><strong>Do not let AI run source selection without disclosure.</strong> Covered on <a href="ai-not-using.html">When NOT to Use AI</a>.</li>
          <li><strong>Verify every regulatory citation.</strong> Models hallucinate them confidently.</li>
          <li><strong>The "use the approved tool" mandate, as written, is slowing the workforce down.</strong> Good policy governs data, not model choice for public work.</li>
          <li><strong>The signature is the decision.</strong> AI helps. You sign.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>

      <p style="font-size:.9rem;color:var(--text-muted);margin-top:1.2rem;">Disagree with any of this? I would rather hear it than not. <a href="contact.html">Send me the pushback.</a></p>

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en" style="--cfm-accent: #f59e0b;"><head>
  <!-- Google tag (gtag.js) -->
  <script async="" src="https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js?id=G-X2RXS78N7K"></script>

  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="Government Purchase Card (GPC) training for new contracting officers. Covers the three uses of the GPC under FAR 13.301, the DAFI 64-117 program structure, prohibitions, and how to use GPC as a payment method for maximum efficiency.">
  <title>Government Purchase Cards | ContractingHQ</title>
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin="">
  <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@300;400;500;600;700;800&family=Rajdhani:wght@500;600;700&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <style>
    /* ── Page shell ── */
    .gpc-bg { background: #040d1f; padding: 0 0 6rem; min-height: 80vh; }

    /* ── Tab bar ── */
    .gpc-tabs { display: flex; gap: 0; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); background: rgba(4,13,31,0.95); position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 90; backdrop-filter: blur(8px); flex-wrap: wrap; }
    .gpc-tab { padding: 0.85rem 1.5rem; font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1px; color: var(--silver); background: none; border: none; border-bottom: 3px solid transparent; cursor: pointer; transition: all 0.18s; font-family: inherit; white-space: nowrap; }
    .gpc-tab:hover { color: var(--white); }
    .gpc-tab.active { color: var(--accent); border-bottom-color: var(--accent); }
    .gpc-panel { display: none; padding: 3rem 1.5rem; max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; }
    .gpc-panel.active { display: block; }

    /* ── Intro ── */
    .gpc-intro { text-align: center; padding: 2.5rem 1.5rem 0; }
    .gpc-intro-tag { display: inline-block; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.25); color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 2px; text-transform: uppercase; padding: 0.25rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 100px; margin-bottom: 0.65rem; }
    .gpc-intro h2 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: clamp(1.4rem,3vw,2rem); font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.4rem; }
    .gpc-intro p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.9rem; max-width: 620px; margin: 0 auto 1.5rem; line-height: 1.6; }

    /* ── Learn ── */
    .learn-section { margin-bottom: 2.5rem; }
    .learn-section h3 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.35rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.75rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }
    .learn-section h3 .section-num { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; width: 30px; height: 30px; border-radius: 8px; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.12); color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; flex-shrink: 0; }
    .learn-body { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.92rem; line-height: 1.75; }
    .learn-body p { margin-bottom: 1rem; }
    .learn-body strong { color: var(--white); font-weight: 600; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box { background: rgba(74,158,255,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); border-radius: 12px; padding: 1rem 1.25rem; margin: 1rem 0; font-size: 0.88rem; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.warn { background: rgba(248,113,113,0.05); border-color: rgba(248,113,113,0.2); }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.warn strong { color: #fca5a5; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.tip { background: rgba(52,211,153,0.05); border-color: rgba(52,211,153,0.2); }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.tip strong { color: #6ee7b7; }
    .learn-divider { border: none; border-top: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.08); margin: 2rem 0; }

    /* ── Criteria list ── */
    .criteria-list { list-style: none; padding: 0; margin: 0.75rem 0; }
    .criteria-list li { padding: 0.25rem 0 0.25rem 1.25rem; position: relative; font-size: 0.88rem; }
    .criteria-list li:before { content: '\2713'; position: absolute; left: 0; color: #6ee7b7; font-weight: 700; }

    /* ── Prohib list (X marks) ── */
    .prohib-list { list-style: none; padding: 0; margin: 0.75rem 0; }
    .prohib-list li { padding: 0.3rem 0 0.3rem 1.25rem; position: relative; font-size: 0.88rem; color: var(--silver); }
    .prohib-list li:before { content: '\2717'; position: absolute; left: 0; color: #fca5a5; font-weight: 700; }

    /* ── Cowboy tip ── */
    .cowboy-tip { background: rgba(251,191,36,0.04); border: 1px solid rgba(251,191,36,0.2); border-radius: 14px; padding: 1.25rem; margin: 1.25rem 0; }
    .cowboy-tip .cowboy-label { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.82rem; font-weight: 700; color: #fbbf24; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1px; margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
    .cowboy-tip p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.88rem; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 0.75rem; }
    .cowboy-tip p:last-child { margin-bottom: 0; }
    .cowboy-tip strong { color: var(--white); }

    /* ── Lookup ── */
    .lookup-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr)); gap: 1.25rem; margin-top: 1.5rem; }
    .lookup-card { background: rgba(10,22,50,0.7); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.12); border-radius: 14px; padding: 1.5rem; transition: all 0.2s; }
    .lookup-card:hover { border-color: rgba(74,158,255,0.3); transform: translateY(-2px); }
    .lookup-card h4 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
    .lookup-card p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.85rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-bottom: 1rem; }
    .lookup-card a { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.4rem; color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; text-decoration: none; transition: all 0.18s; }
    .lookup-card a:hover { color: var(--white); }
    .lookup-card a::after { content: '\2197'; font-size: 0.9rem; }

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      .gpc-tab { padding: 0.7rem 0.9rem; font-size: 0.75rem; }
      .lookup-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
    }
    .bmc-btn{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:.4rem;background:#FFDD00;color:#000;border-radius:8px;padding:.45rem 1rem;font-weight:700;font-size:.83rem;text-decoration:none;transition:opacity .2s,transform .15s}.bmc-btn:hover{opacity:.88;transform:translateY(-1px)}
  </style>

.cfm-brand {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;

}
.cfm-brand-logo {

}
.cfm-brand-logo span { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-on-air {

  text-transform: uppercase; color: #ef4444;
  background: rgba(239,68,68,0.12); border: 1px solid rgba(239,68,68,0.3);

  transition: color 0.3s, background 0.3s, border-color 0.3s;
}
.cfm-on-air.off-air {

}

.cfm-song-info {

}

  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  transition: background 0.3s;
}
.cfm-meta { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-meta-title {
  font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 600; color: #e2e8f0;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-sub {
  font-size: 0.68rem; color: #556; margin-top: 0.1rem;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-genre {
  display: inline-block; font-size: 0.6rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff);
  background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border-radius: 3px;
  padding: 0.1rem 0.35rem; margin-top: 0.15rem; letter-spacing: 0.5px;
}
.cfm-heart {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1rem;
  color: #445; transition: color 0.2s, transform 0.15s; flex-shrink: 0; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-heart.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-heart:hover { transform: scale(1.2); }

.cfm-controls {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1.25rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0.4rem;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: color 0.18s, background 0.18s, transform 0.15s;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  width: 30px; height: 30px;
}
.cfm-btn:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn {
  width: 38px; height: 38px; font-size: 1rem;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); color: #040d1f;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: all 0.18s;
}
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn:hover { transform: scale(1.08); filter: brightness(1.15); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-active { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }

.cfm-progress-zone {
  flex: 1; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.6rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; min-width: 0;
}
.cfm-time { font-size: 0.68rem; color: #445; flex-shrink: 0; min-width: 32px; }
.cfm-time.right { text-align: right; }
.cfm-bar-wrap { flex: 1; position: relative; height: 4px; cursor: pointer; }
.cfm-bar-bg {
  position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
}
.cfm-bar-fill {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; bottom: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); width: 0%; transition: width 0.1s linear;
}
.cfm-bar-thumb {
  position: absolute; top: 50%; width: 12px; height: 12px;
  border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
  opacity: 0; transition: opacity 0.18s; box-shadow: 0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.4);
  left: 0%;
}
.cfm-bar-wrap:hover .cfm-bar-thumb { opacity: 1; }

.cfm-volume-zone {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1rem; border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-vol-icon { font-size: 0.75rem; color: #445; cursor: pointer; }
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider {
  -webkit-appearance: none; appearance: none;
  width: 70px; height: 3px; border-radius: 3px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); outline: none; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-webkit-slider-thumb {
  -webkit-appearance: none; width: 16px; height: 16px; border-radius: 50%;
  background: #fff; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-moz-range-thumb {
  width: 12px; height: 12px; border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; cursor: pointer; border: none;
}

.cfm-playlist-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0 1rem;
  transition: color 0.18s; flex-shrink: 0; height: 100%;
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.35rem; font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-playlist-btn:hover { color: #fff; }
.cfm-playlist-btn.open { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-playlist-text { font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; }
.cfm-playlist-count {
  display: inline-grid; place-items: center;
  min-width: 1.35rem; height: 1.35rem; padding: 0 0.28rem;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 800;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle {
  position: relative;
  height: 100%;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  padding: 0 0.85rem;
  border: none;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  background: rgba(217,154,49,0.04);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  flex-shrink: 0;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle span {
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.28);
  border-radius: 999px;
  padding: 0.22rem 0.52rem;
  color: #d99a31;
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 900;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover span,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible span,
.cfm-cco-toggle.active span {
  color: #080905;
  background: #d99a31;
  border-color: #d99a31;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after {
  content: attr(data-tip);
  position: absolute;
  right: 0.5rem;
  bottom: calc(100% + 10px);
  width: min(300px, calc(100vw - 24px));
  padding: 0.65rem 0.75rem;
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.34);
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: rgba(6,3,16,0.96);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  box-shadow: 0 14px 34px rgba(0,0,0,0.42);
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 650;
  line-height: 1.45;
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
  transform: translateY(4px);
  transition: opacity 0.16s ease, transform 0.16s ease;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover::after,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible::after {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle::after {
  content: none !important;
  display: none !important;
}

/* Playlist drawer */
#cfm-drawer {
  position: fixed; bottom: 68px; right: 0;
  width: 380px; max-height: min(560px, calc(100vh - 92px));
  background: #080414;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  border-radius: 14px 0 0 0;
  overflow-y: auto; z-index: 9998;
  display: none;
  box-shadow: -4px -4px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.5);
}
#cfm-drawer.open { display: block; }
.cfm-drawer-hdr {
  position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 1;
  padding: 0.85rem 1rem 0.75rem;
  background: #080414;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-drawer-title-row {
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 0.75rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-title {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.2px;
}
.cfm-drawer-count { color: #556; font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; white-space: nowrap; }
.cfm-drawer-actions {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.45rem; margin-top: 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  padding: 0.35rem 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.active { color: #ef4444; border-color: rgba(239,68,68,0.34); background: rgba(239,68,68,0.08); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.disabled { opacity: 0.45; cursor: default; }
.cfm-drawer-empty {
  padding: 1rem;
  color: #8a9bb0;
  font-size: 0.82rem;
  line-height: 1.55;
}
.cfm-track-item {
  display: grid; grid-template-columns: 22px minmax(0, 1fr) auto auto; align-items: center; gap: 0.65rem;
  padding: 0.65rem 1rem; cursor: pointer;
  background: #080414;
  transition: background 0.15s; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.04);
}
.cfm-track-item:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); }
.cfm-track-item.active { background: #11172d; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped { opacity: 0.58; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped .cfm-track-name { text-decoration: line-through; }
.cfm-track-marker {
  display: grid; place-items: center;
  width: 22px; min-width: 22px;
}
.cfm-track-num {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.8rem; color: #334;
  min-width: 18px; text-align: center;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-num { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-track-dot {
  width: 8px; height: 8px; border-radius: 50%;
  animation: cfm-pulse 1s ease-in-out infinite; flex-shrink: 0;
  display: none;
}
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-dot { display: block; }
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-num { display: none; }
.cfm-track-info { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-track-name {
  font-size: 0.82rem; font-weight: 600; color: #c0cdd8;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-name { color: #fff; }
.cfm-track-genre { font-size: 0.67rem; color: #445; margin-top: 0.1rem; }
.cfm-track-fav {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #334; transition: color 0.18s; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-track-fav.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-track-skip {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #66758a;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.64rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1;
  padding: 0.32rem 0.48rem;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.cfm-track-skip:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
.cfm-track-skip.active { color: #f59e0b; border-color: rgba(245,158,11,0.34); background: rgba(245,158,11,0.08); }

#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar-track { background: transparent; }
