}
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(1) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 1.1s ease-in-out infinite; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(2) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 0.9s ease-in-out infinite 0.1s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(3) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 1.2s ease-in-out infinite 0.16s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(4) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 0.84s ease-in-out infinite 0.08s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(5) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 1.15s ease-in-out infinite 0.18s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(6) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 0.96s ease-in-out infinite 0.14s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(7) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 1.18s ease-in-out infinite 0.06s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span:nth-child(8) { animation: cfm-sb-eq 1.02s ease-in-out infinite 0.12s; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-ring { animation: cfm-sb-spin 7s linear infinite; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-ring.cfm-sb-art-ring-b { animation-duration: 4.4s; animation-direction: reverse; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-orbital.cfm-sb-orbital-a { animation: cfm-sb-orbit-a 6s linear infinite; }
.cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-orbital.cfm-sb-orbital-b { animation: cfm-sb-orbit-b 7.4s linear infinite reverse; }
@keyframes cfm-sb-glow { 0%,100% { box-shadow: inset 0 0 40px rgba(74,158,255,0.07); } 50% { box-shadow: inset 0 0 80px rgba(74,158,255,0.14); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-eq { 0%,100% { transform: scaleY(0.6); } 50% { transform: scaleY(1.12); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-spin { from { transform: rotate(0deg); } to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
@keyframes cfm-sb-orbit-a {
  0%   { transform: translate(0, 0); }
  25%  { transform: translate(14px, 8px); }
  50%  { transform: translate(32px, 26px); }
  75%  { transform: translate(10px, 46px); }
  100% { transform: translate(0, 0); }
}
@keyframes cfm-sb-orbit-b {
  0%   { transform: translate(0, 0); }
  25%  { transform: translate(-12px, -8px); }
  50%  { transform: translate(-28px, -22px); }
  75%  { transform: translate(-8px, -42px); }
  100% { transform: translate(0, 0); }
}
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .cfm-sb-art.playing,
  .cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-eq span,
  .cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-ring,
  .cfm-sb-art.playing .cfm-sb-art-orbital {
    animation: none !important;
  }
}

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="container">
    <span class="hero-badge">Customer Education</span>
    <h1 class="page-hero-title">The Why Behind the Buy</h1>
    <p class="page-hero-sub">The candid answers to the questions your program office keeps asking about contracting. None of this is the official line. All of it is what I would tell you over coffee.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="article-bg">
  <div class="article-wrap">

    <div class="breadcrumb">
      <a href="index.html">Home</a>
      <span class="breadcrumb-sep">/</span>
      <a href="customer-education.html">Customer Education</a>
      <span class="breadcrumb-sep">/</span>
      <span class="breadcrumb-current">The Why Behind the Buy</span>
    </div>

    <div class="article">

      <p><strong>Once you send your requirement, it's only the beginning.</strong> Solicit, evaluate, award, admin. An entire process kicks off the moment your package lands with contracting.</p>

      <p>Quick deployment story: a program office walked a package over to me and on the way out one of them said "it's ordered!" That package had not even hit solicitation yet. The rest of this page answers the questions customers keep asking about everything that happens after you hit send.</p>

      <div class="qindex">
        <h3>In this guide</h3>
        <ol>
          <li><a href="#q-requirements">Why do we need clearly defined requirements?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-team">When you send the package, you join the acquisition team</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-vagueness">What actually breaks when requirements are vague?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-solesource">Why do we try to avoid sole source?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-salient">What are salient characteristics and how do I find them?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-gsa">Is GSA really mandated?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-overspending">The myth of government overspending</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-partner">What could I do to be a better partner for contracting?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-beginning">Start from the beginning of developing a requirement</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-market">How market research should be done</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-pushback">Why does your CO push back?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-dontknow">When should I tell the CO "I don't know how to define this"?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-misalignment">Why your needs and the CO's needs sometimes disagree</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-smallbiz">Why do we go to small business?</a></li>
          <li><a href="#q-stonewall">How do I get past a CO who is stonewalling my requirement?</a></li>
        </ol>
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-requirements"><span class="q-num">01</span>Why do we need clearly defined requirements?</h2>

      <p>The moment a requirement is ambiguous, three problems show up at the same time. Pricing gets unreliable because every vendor is bidding on a slightly different thing. Evaluation gets messy because you cannot compare apples when half the offers are oranges. And acceptance gets contentious because the contract does not clearly say what "done" looks like.</p>

      <p>A clearly defined requirement tells every offeror the same story. It tells the CO what to write into the evaluation factors. It tells the winner what they are on the hook for. It tells the COR and the program office what to inspect at delivery. When the requirement is ambiguous, each of those roles ends up guessing, and every one of those guesses is a potential dispute later.</p>

      <p>If your requirement is "we need better analytics," your contract is going to be a mess. If your requirement is "we need a cloud-based analytics platform that supports these specific use cases, at this performance level, accessible by these users, for this period," your contract has a fighting chance of ending cleanly.</p>

      <div class="pull-quote">
        If a vendor has to ask "what do you mean by that?", your requirement is not clear yet.
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-team"><span class="q-num">02</span>When you send the package, you join the acquisition team</h2>

      <p>The word "customer" does not capture what actually happens when you send a package to contracting. Nobody walks into a contracting office and says "I would like one contract, please." When you send a requirement, you are joining the acquisition team for that buy, and you own it alongside the CO from that point forward.</p>

      <p>From the CO's perspective, you are now the technical expert on this requirement, whether you came in feeling like one or not. Your name is on the package. You answer the technical questions that come back from vendors. You attend the meetings. You sit on the evaluation panel and read proposals. You help shape the evaluation factors. You help design the quality assurance plan, because the COR and the program office are the ones who will actually measure performance after award. All of that work belongs to the acquisition team, and you are on the team.</p>

      <p>This is not a soft ask. Acquisitions where the requester is engaged and invested produce better outcomes at almost every step. Acquisitions where the requester sends the package and disappears produce defensible but blunt outcomes. If you do not participate in shaping the strategy, you default to lowest price that technically meets your specification. That may be fine. It may also miss the thing you actually wanted.</p>

      <p>Here is where I want you, as a partner, to show up:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>Acquisition strategy.</strong> Lowest price or best-value tradeoff? What is worth paying more for, and what is not?</li>
        <li><strong>Evaluation factors.</strong> What are we actually scoring on, and what weight does each factor carry? You will be reading the proposals, so you should have a hand in writing the scorecard.</li>
        <li><strong>Quality assurance.</strong> How will we know the contractor is delivering? What metrics, what inspection frequency, what cure paths? You and your COR will live with this after award, so it should look the way you need it to.</li>
        <li><strong>Source selection.</strong> Reading the proposals, asking the clarification questions, scoring against the factors you helped write.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>The CO still owns the file, and there are moments where the CO has to overrule a specific ask because the FAR or the agency supplement requires it. That is fine. A CO working with an engaged partner can make the buy look like what the program actually needs. A CO working in a vacuum cannot.</p>

      <div class="practice-box">
        <span class="practice-title">The deal</span>
        <p><strong>If you are not going to participate, you get what you get and you don't throw a fit.</strong> Lowest price, technically acceptable, chosen by the CO without your input. That is the default when the requester opts out. If you want the buy to reflect what you actually need, you have to be on the team.</p>
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-vagueness"><span class="q-num">03</span>What actually breaks when requirements are vague?</h2>

      <p>Zoom in on a vague requirement and you can watch the damage accumulate at every phase of the acquisition.</p>

      <p><strong>Market research.</strong> Vendors read the same sentence and respond with five completely different products. The CO cannot tell which one is closest to what you wanted, because the sentence did not tell them.</p>

      <p><strong>Solicitation.</strong> The CO has to translate your requirement into an evaluation section. A vague requirement forces vague evaluation factors, which means the CO cannot meaningfully score responses. Either the factors get padded with subjective criteria that invite protests, or the acquisition defaults to lowest price, which may not be what you wanted at all.</p>

      <p><strong>Evaluation.</strong> Proposals come back looking like they are solving different problems. Comparing them apples-to-apples becomes impossible. The cheapest offer is probably the one that interpreted the requirement loosest, and the most expensive is probably the one that guessed most conservatively. Both can be reasonable and still neither lands on what you actually needed.</p>

      <p><strong>Award.</strong> You are locked into the strategy you picked at the start. You cannot change strategies mid-acquisition. If the requirement was vague when the strategy was chosen, the foundation was already shaky, and now you have two options. Award against the criteria you wrote and accept that you may not be buying what you needed. Or cancel the acquisition and start the process over, which can add months and sometimes push the buy out of fiscal year entirely.</p>

      <p><strong>Administration.</strong> The contractor delivers what the contract says. If the contract is vague, "what the contract says" is contested ground. You want X, they delivered Y, and both sides have a defensible reading of the page. The COR's life gets hard. Your program's schedule slips. Amendments to clarify scope are expensive.</p>

      <p>Every one of those costs shows up in time, money, or mission, usually all three. The investment in nailing the requirement before the solicitation is almost always cheaper than cleaning up a vague one after award.</p>

      <h2 id="q-solesource"><span class="q-num">04</span>Why do we try to avoid sole source?</h2>

      <p>Competition is the default for a reason, and the reason is not paperwork for its own sake. Three offers gives you price discovery, a quality signal, and protest resistance. One offer gives you the price that vendor wants you to pay, and not much leverage to push back on any of it.</p>

      <p>Sole source is not illegal. It is legally allowed under the FAR's exceptions to full and open competition, and there are plenty of legitimate reasons to use it. What it does is shift the burden. You have to justify why no other source will work. You have to document it. Someone senior has to sign. The file has to survive review, and sometimes a protest.</p>

      <p>Program offices sometimes land on sole source because they already know and like the vendor. That is a preference, not a justification. The CO is not being difficult when they push back on it; they are testing whether we can buy this competitively first, because if we can, we must. Competition is the default the FAR requires, and sole source is the narrow exception.</p>

      <p>Worth knowing: everything we solicit gets posted publicly. A sole-source justification goes up on SAM.gov for the whole market to read, and your competitors will read it. A weak justification (we already have a good relationship with them, they made it through last time, we like working with them) gets picked apart in public. Protests get filed. Awards get sustained. Packages come back for rework. The speed you were trying to protect by sole-sourcing evaporates.</p>

      <p>If your product really does have only one source, say so and show it. The J&A process exists exactly for that. Just do not expect "I already know who I want" to survive public review.</p>

      <h2 id="q-salient"><span class="q-num">05</span>What are salient characteristics and how do I find them?</h2>

      <p>Salient characteristics are the testable features of a product or service that describe what you actually need, without naming a specific vendor or brand. They are how you stay competitive when you already have a favorite product in your head.</p>

      <p>The phrase comes up most when a program office says "I need Brand X." The CO cannot just buy Brand X. Buying a brand by name means sole source, which means justification, senior approval, and a paper trail. Salient characteristics let you describe the thing without sole-sourcing. Instead of "Brand X Widget," you describe a widget that handles 12 amps, fits a 2U rack, supports IPv6, carries a five-year warranty, and ships within 30 days. Any vendor meeting those characteristics can compete. The CO runs a real competition. Brand X is welcome to win on the merits.</p>

      <p>How to find the salient characteristics of what you need:</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Start with the mission. What does this thing have to do for the program?</li>
        <li>List every feature you are actually using on the reference product. Not the marketing bullets. The features you touch.</li>
        <li>Separate must-haves from nice-to-haves. The must-haves are candidates for salient characteristics. The nice-to-haves are not.</li>
        <li>For each must-have, ask whether it is mission-essential or whether it is habit. Habit features are how brochures get written into requirements.</li>
        <li>Sanity-check the market. If nobody else can meet the characteristics you wrote down, that is useful information. The requirement may legitimately be sole source, and the J&A route is the honest one.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>Salient characteristics are the bridge between "I know what product I have been using" and "the CO can buy a product that meets my need in a defensible way." The more honest and specific the list, the stronger the file around the buy.</p>

      <div class="pull-quote">
        "I need Brand X" is a starting point for a conversation, not an ending point for a requirement.
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-gsa"><span class="q-num">06</span>Is GSA really mandated?</h2>

      <p>Mostly no, despite how often you hear it said.</p>

      <p>The FAR establishes an order of preference for supplies and services. GSA schedules are one of the preferred options under Part 8 in specific situations. Some agencies layer on a supplement that says "use GSA first" within certain scope. None of that adds up to a universal mandate for every buy.</p>

      <p>In practice, you have options. GSA Schedules. GSA Advantage for commercial items. Open-market competitive buys under Part 12 or Part 13. Existing IDIQs. Agency BPAs. Which one is best depends on price, competition, lead time, and how well the vehicle fits the requirement. Sometimes GSA wins the analysis. Sometimes it does not.</p>

      <p>Where GSA earns its reputation: speed and administrative cost. A buy that would take 90 days on the open market can close in under 30 on a Schedule. Under the Simplified Acquisition Threshold ($350K as of this writing), a GSA requirement can usually be turned around in a week or two. If you bring three GSA quotes with the package, that window shrinks to days. That is why program offices reach for GSA, and when the fit is right, it is a strong choice.</p>

      <p>"It has to be GSA" is an answer you should be able to get a citation for if someone is telling you that. When you ask for the citation, the answer often turns into "it is easier on GSA" or "my office prefers GSA." Both of those are fine reasons to pick GSA when it fits. Neither of them is a mandate.</p>

      <h2 id="q-overspending"><span class="q-num">07</span>The myth of government overspending</h2>

      <p>You have heard the stories. Hundred-dollar hammers. Ten-thousand-dollar toilet seats. The general sense that government always pays three times what a thing should cost.</p>

      <p>Most of those stories are either old outliers that got reported badly, or they are specialized parts where the real price reflects what it cost to certify, test, and source a specific component to a specific documentation standard. A commercial toilet seat and a pressurized-aircraft toilet seat with redundant seals, traceable material certifications, and a twenty-year replacement window are not the same product.</p>

      <p>The social media version of this runs year-round. A post goes viral with a photo of a $10,000 piece of hardware and a caption about wasteful government spending. Nine times out of ten, the post is missing the context that made the price reasonable. I have seen a $10,000 printer cited as an outrage, and the actual contract included unlimited ink and toner for five years. The price was a steal. The post did not mention the ink. Those posts travel fast because outrage travels fast, and the full context rarely travels with them.</p>

      <p>Where government really does pay more, the reasons are usually legible. Specialized requirements. Low-volume production runs. Test and certification overhead. Compliance carrying costs. Specifications that programs ask for because somebody's life or mission depends on the thing working. All of that shows up in the price, and it should.</p>

      <p>The version that matters day to day: government buys commercial things at close to commercial prices, usually with a bit of overhead for process. Government buys specialized things at prices that reflect the specialization. The hammer story is a meme, not the day job.</p>

      <h2 id="q-partner"><span class="q-num">08</span>What could I do to be a better partner for contracting?</h2>

      <p>The single biggest thing you can do: give your CO more lead time.</p>

      <p>A package that arrives six months before your need-date lets the CO run a proper acquisition. A package that arrives two weeks before need-date forces a rushed strategy that costs you options and often costs you money. The CO cannot compress solicitation periods, evaluation time, or review cycles past a certain point without creating real risk on the file.</p>

      <p>Beyond lead time, these are the moves that actually move the needle:</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Know your funding when you send the package. Color of money, fiscal year, what is authorized.</li>
        <li>Bring a realistic IGCE. Not an aspirational one.</li>
        <li>Come with a clear picture of what you want and a real openness on how to get there.</li>
        <li>Pick up the phone before you send the PR. A fifteen-minute call can save days of clarification ping-pong later.</li>
        <li>Tell the CO about your preferred vendor early. Let them route it correctly instead of discovering a sole-source flag halfway through solicitation.</li>
        <li>Ask "what would make your file easier to defend?" The CO's file is your shared problem, not the CO's alone.</li>
        <li>Be reachable during evaluation. If clarifications come through, a same-day response can keep the schedule alive.</li>
        <li>Listen when the CO pushes back. The pushback is almost always protecting you from something downstream.</li>
        <li>When you disagree, have the conversation with your CO. Do not shop for a second opinion at a different CO down the hall.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>None of this is hard. It just takes a habit of starting earlier and treating contracting like a real phase of the project, not a vending machine at the end of it.</p>

      <div class="practice-box">
        <span class="practice-title">If you only remember one thing</span>
        <p><strong>Start the conversation with your CO six months before you need the contract.</strong> Not the package. The conversation. Every other problem on this page gets easier when the CO is in the room early.</p>
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-beginning"><span class="q-num">09</span>Start from the beginning of developing a requirement</h2>

      <p>Most bad requirements start because somebody wrote the product spec before they wrote the problem statement.</p>

      <p>Start with the mission or outcome. What are you actually trying to accomplish? What does "done" look like for your program? Once you know the problem, you can ask who in the market solves it. Once you know who solves it, you can ask how they solve it. Once you know how they solve it, the product or service spec writes itself.</p>

      <p>If you write the product spec first, you will end up with a requirement that looks suspiciously like the last vendor's brochure. That is how sole-source-by-accident happens. That is also how protests happen, because competitors read the requirement, recognize it, and file.</p>

      <p>Order of operations: mission, problem, outcome, market capabilities, then requirement. Not the other way around.</p>

      <h2 id="q-market"><span class="q-num">10</span>How market research should be done</h2>

      <p>Market research is the step that everyone skips, and the step everyone should do.</p>

      <p>What market research is not: reading one company's website and writing a requirement that matches their product.</p>

      <p>What market research is:</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Identifying who in the market can actually solve the problem you have.</li>
        <li>Looking at what they offer, how they price, and under what contract vehicles.</li>
        <li>Talking to more than one source. RFIs and sources-sought notices are built for this.</li>
        <li>Checking what the government has bought recently through USAspending, FPDS, and SAM.gov awards.</li>
        <li>Noting whether small businesses can do this work.</li>
        <li>Writing it down. A market research report is not optional. It is the record of the decisions that shaped your acquisition strategy.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>Good market research protects you. It tells the CO "yes, I looked, and here is why I am asking for what I am asking for." Thin market research tells the CO you wrote to a specific vendor and did not check. The file has to show one of those things, and only one of them is defensible.</p>

      <h2 id="q-pushback"><span class="q-num">11</span>Why does your CO push back?</h2>

      <p>Because the signature on the contract is theirs, and the regulatory and legal liability is theirs. If the acquisition goes sideways (sustained protest, CPARS dispute, IG finding, Congressional inquiry), the CO is the one writing the response.</p>

      <p>When a CO pushes back on your requirement, they are not being difficult. They are doing the job. They see the risks you do not see because they see them every day across a dozen requirements. They read protest decisions for fun. They have watched a program office get the same thing wrong three times in a row and want to keep yours from being the fourth.</p>

      <p>The best thing you can do with pushback is ask a different question: "what would it take to make this work?" That moves the conversation from adversarial to collaborative. Nine times out of ten, the CO can tell you exactly what they need in the package to proceed. The tenth time is where supervisors get involved, and even then, it is rarely about obstruction.</p>

      <div class="pull-quote">
        "What would it take to make this work?" turns a wall into a conversation.
      </div>

      <h2 id="q-dontknow"><span class="q-num">12</span>When should I tell the CO "I don't know how to define this"?</h2>

      <p>Saying "I don't know how to define this, I really need help" is one of the most useful things a customer can hand a CO. It redirects the acquisition onto a path built for uncertainty, instead of forcing a vague requirement into a process that expects clarity.</p>

      <p>Here is what opens up on the CO side when a customer is honest about where they are:</p>

      <ul>
        <li><strong>You know the outcome but not the solution.</strong> The CO can reach for a Commercial Solutions Opening or a similar innovation-focused vehicle. Those are designed for problems where industry knows how to solve it and you do not need to prescribe how.</li>
        <li><strong>You know the capability you want but not who makes it.</strong> The CO can issue an RFI or a sources-sought notice so the market can raise its hand before a specification ever gets written.</li>
        <li><strong>You have a rough spec but cannot tell whether it is realistic.</strong> The CO can set up one-on-one meetings with vendors ahead of the solicitation so the market can sanity-check your asks.</li>
        <li><strong>You cannot separate must-have from nice-to-have.</strong> The CO can pull in an engineer, a SME from another program office, or an in-house tech evaluator to work through the list with you.</li>
        <li><strong>You do not know if a small business can do this.</strong> Ask. The CO can point you at recent awards and small-business capability statements in that NAICS before anyone writes a Rule of Two memo.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>The trap is pretending you have a clean requirement when you do not. That produces a brittle spec, which produces a solicitation that does not reflect what you actually need, which produces a contract that misses the target. By the time you notice, you are modifying the contract post-award, which is slower and more expensive than every one of the paths above.</p>

      <p>Honesty up front is a shortcut. Say you need help. Let the CO pick the path.</p>

      <h2 id="q-misalignment"><span class="q-num">13</span>Why your needs and the CO's needs sometimes disagree</h2>

      <p>Because you are optimizing for different things, and both of you are right.</p>

      <p>You need: speed, the specific capability, predictable timelines, the vendor your team already trusts.</p>

      <p>The CO needs: competition, a defensible file, compliance with the FAR and agency supplements, adequate review time, and a contract that does not fall apart in year two.</p>

      <p>Both of those are legitimate, and they will not always point at the same answer. That friction is the system working as designed. The tension between "I want this now" and "I have to be able to defend this later" is what keeps both of you out of trouble at the end.</p>

      <p>The partnership gets strong when the customer understands why the CO asks what they ask, and the CO understands why the customer has the timeline they have. Nothing magical. Just mutual translation.</p>

      <h2 id="q-smallbiz"><span class="q-num">14</span>Why do we go to small business?</h2>

      <p>Because the market is stronger when small businesses are in it, and because Congress and the FAR have decided that is worth protecting.</p>

      <p>The policy framework is substantial. Part 19 of the FAR sets it up. SBA size standards define what counts as small. Agency small business goals push offices to hit specific percentages. Set-asides (small business, WOSB, SDVOSB, HUBZone, 8(a)) route specific opportunities to specific categories. The Rule of Two, now at FAR 19.502, says that if there is a reasonable expectation that two or more small businesses will bid at fair market prices, the buy gets set aside.</p>

      <p>Beyond the policy, there is a practical reason. Small businesses are often how new capability enters the federal market. They are often more flexible, more responsive, and more willing to shape their work to a specific customer's problem. The government's pipeline of mid-size and large primes depends on a healthy small-business base underneath it.</p>

      <p>The customer version: if you are early in shaping a requirement and a small business could do this work, lean into it. If a small business set-aside is legally required, the CO is going to tell you. Make that easier on them, not harder.</p>

      <h2 id="q-stonewall"><span class="q-num">15</span>How do I get past a CO who is stonewalling my requirement?</h2>

      <p>First, confirm whether it is actually stonewalling. Most of what gets called stonewalling is the CO asking for something the package is missing, or flagging a risk that has not been addressed. Ask the CO directly: "what specifically would need to change or arrive for this to move forward?" Get the answer in writing.</p>

      <p>If the answer tells you what to fix, fix it.</p>

      <p>If the answer does not tell you anything useful, or you get radio silence, try these in order:</p>

      <ul>
        <li>Your supervisor talking to their supervisor. Calm, in writing, with the chronology of the request.</li>
        <li>Your office's contracting ombudsman or equivalent if one exists.</li>
        <li>The acquisition lead at your senior command or agency level if the situation truly warrants it.</li>
      </ul>

      <p>One option worth knowing about is what people call CO shopping. Different COs have different risk tolerances, and a more experienced or less risk-averse CO may be willing to take on a project another CO has declined. There is a polite way to ask for this: have your supervisor contact the CO's supervisor, on the record, and ask whether another CO could take a second look at the package. Do not do this secretly, and do not walk CO-to-CO in the hallway hoping the second one does not notice. That path gets packages rescinded and working relationships destroyed. Your CO's colleagues talk to each other.</p>

      <p>Even when you ask the right way, do not count on it. It depends heavily on manning, on whether another CO has the bandwidth, and on office egos. If nobody else is available, you are at the mercy of your current CO's judgment on the file. Sometimes that is the final answer.</p>

      <p>The vast majority of the time, what looks like stonewalling is a CO trying to keep you from making a defensible bad decision. The times when it is real obstruction are rare, and when they happen, they resolve at the supervisor level, not at the CO level.</p>

      <h2>The honest closing</h2>

      <p>None of this is a manual for getting around your CO. It is the opposite. The best acquisitions I have ever worked happened when the customer understood what I needed and when, and I understood what they needed and when, and both of us treated the other as the partner we actually are.</p>

      <p>That partnership does not start on the day the package hits the inbox. It starts six months earlier, when the program office has its first "what do we actually need?" conversation and brings the CO in. The sooner, the better. The more honest, the better. The more each side understands the other's job, the better the contract reads at the end.</p>

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en" style="--cfm-accent: #d97706;"><head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
  <meta name="description" content="Learn how PSC/FSC codes work in government contracting. Interactive decision aid, practice scenarios, and external lookup tools for contracting officers.">
  <title>PSC / FSC Codes | ContractingHQ</title>
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
  <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin="">
  <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter:wght@300;400;500;600;700;800&family=Rajdhani:wght@500;600;700&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <style>
    /* ── Page shell ── */
    .fsc-bg { background: #040d1f; padding: 0 0 6rem; min-height: 80vh; }

    /* ── Tab bar ── */
    .fsc-tabs { display: flex; gap: 0; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); background: rgba(4,13,31,0.95); position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 90; backdrop-filter: blur(8px); flex-wrap: wrap; }
    .fsc-tab { padding: 0.85rem 1.5rem; font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1px; color: var(--silver); background: none; border: none; border-bottom: 3px solid transparent; cursor: pointer; transition: all 0.18s; font-family: inherit; white-space: nowrap; }
    .fsc-tab:hover { color: var(--white); }
    .fsc-tab.active { color: var(--accent); border-bottom-color: var(--accent); }
    .fsc-panel { display: none; padding: 3rem 1.5rem; max-width: 900px; margin: 0 auto; }
    .fsc-panel.active { display: block; }

    /* ── Intro badge ── */
    .fsc-intro { text-align: center; padding: 2.5rem 1.5rem 0; }
    .fsc-intro-tag { display: inline-block; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.25); color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 2px; text-transform: uppercase; padding: 0.25rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 100px; margin-bottom: 0.65rem; }
    .fsc-intro h2 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: clamp(1.4rem,3vw,2rem); font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.4rem; }
    .fsc-intro p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.9rem; max-width: 520px; margin: 0 auto 1.5rem; line-height: 1.6; }

    /* ── Learn section ── */
    .learn-section { margin-bottom: 2.5rem; }
    .learn-section h3 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.35rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.75rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }
    .learn-section h3 .section-num { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; width: 30px; height: 30px; border-radius: 8px; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.12); color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; flex-shrink: 0; }
    .learn-body { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.92rem; line-height: 1.75; }
    .learn-body p { margin-bottom: 1rem; }
    .learn-body strong { color: var(--white); font-weight: 600; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box { background: rgba(74,158,255,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); border-radius: 12px; padding: 1rem 1.25rem; margin: 1rem 0; font-size: 0.88rem; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.warn { background: rgba(248,113,113,0.05); border-color: rgba(248,113,113,0.2); }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.warn strong { color: #fca5a5; }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.tip { background: rgba(52,211,153,0.05); border-color: rgba(52,211,153,0.2); }
    .learn-body .highlight-box.tip strong { color: #6ee7b7; }
    .learn-body .far-ref { color: var(--accent); font-weight: 600; font-size: 0.82rem; font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; letter-spacing: 0.5px; }
    .learn-divider { border: none; border-top: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.08); margin: 2rem 0; }

    /* ── Decision Aid ── */
    .da-prompt { text-align: center; margin-bottom: 2rem; }
    .da-prompt h3 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.5rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
    .da-prompt p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.9rem; }

    .da-options { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; margin-bottom: 2rem; }
    .da-option { background: rgba(10,22,50,0.7); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.12); border-radius: 14px; padding: 1.5rem; cursor: pointer; transition: all 0.2s; text-align: center; }
    .da-option:hover { border-color: rgba(74,158,255,0.35); background: rgba(74,158,255,0.06); transform: translateY(-2px); }
    .da-option.selected { border-color: var(--accent); background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); box-shadow: 0 0 20px rgba(74,158,255,0.1); }
    .da-option-icon { font-size: 2.5rem; margin-bottom: 0.75rem; display: block; }
    .da-option-label { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.15rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.35rem; }
    .da-option-sub { font-size: 0.8rem; color: var(--silver); line-height: 1.5; }

    .da-result { display: none; background: rgba(10,22,50,0.7); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); border-radius: 14px; padding: 2rem; animation: fadeSlideUp 0.35s ease-out; }
    .da-result.visible { display: block; }
    .da-result h4 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.2rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--accent); margin-bottom: 1rem; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem; }
    .da-result p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.9rem; line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 0.75rem; }
    .da-result strong { color: var(--white); }
    .da-result .da-series { display: inline-block; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.12); color: var(--accent); font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-weight: 700; font-size: 1.1rem; padding: 0.3rem 0.9rem; border-radius: 8px; margin: 0.5rem 0; }
    .da-result .da-caution { background: rgba(248,113,113,0.05); border: 1px solid rgba(248,113,113,0.15); border-radius: 10px; padding: 0.85rem 1rem; margin-top: 1rem; font-size: 0.85rem; color: #fca5a5; line-height: 1.6; }
    .da-result .da-caution strong { color: #fca5a5; }
    .da-reset { display: none; margin-top: 1.5rem; text-align: center; }
    .da-reset.visible { display: block; }
    .da-reset button { padding: 0.55rem 1.4rem; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.25); background: rgba(74,158,255,0.08); color: var(--silver); cursor: pointer; font-family: inherit; transition: all 0.18s; }
    .da-reset button:hover { background: rgba(74,158,255,0.18); color: var(--white); }

    @keyframes fadeSlideUp {
      from { opacity: 0; transform: translateY(12px); }
      to { opacity: 1; transform: translateY(0); }
    }

    /* ── Lookup section ── */
    .lookup-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr)); gap: 1.25rem; margin-top: 1.5rem; }
    .lookup-card { background: rgba(10,22,50,0.7); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.12); border-radius: 14px; padding: 1.5rem; transition: all 0.2s; }
    .lookup-card:hover { border-color: rgba(74,158,255,0.3); transform: translateY(-2px); }
    .lookup-card h4 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
    .lookup-card p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.85rem; line-height: 1.6; margin-bottom: 1rem; }
    .lookup-card a { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.4rem; color: var(--accent); font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; text-decoration: none; transition: all 0.18s; }
    .lookup-card a:hover { color: var(--white); }
    .lookup-card a::after { content: '\2197'; font-size: 0.9rem; }

    /* ── Quiz section ── */
    .quiz-header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1.5rem; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 0.5rem; }
    .quiz-score { font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--accent); letter-spacing: 1px; text-transform: uppercase; }
    .quiz-progress-bar { width: 100%; height: 4px; background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border-radius: 99px; margin-bottom: 2rem; }
    .quiz-progress-fill { height: 100%; background: var(--accent); border-radius: 99px; transition: width 0.3s; }
    .quiz-question { background: rgba(10,22,50,0.7); border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.12); border-radius: 14px; padding: 1.75rem; margin-bottom: 1.5rem; }
    .quiz-q-label { font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 1.5px; text-transform: uppercase; color: var(--accent); margin-bottom: 0.6rem; }
    .quiz-q-text { font-size: 1rem; color: var(--white); line-height: 1.7; margin-bottom: 1rem; }
    .quiz-choices { display: grid; gap: 0.65rem; }
    .quiz-choice { padding: 0.85rem 1.2rem; border-radius: 10px; border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.15); background: rgba(10,22,50,0.6); color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.9rem; font-weight: 600; cursor: pointer; text-align: left; font-family: inherit; transition: all 0.18s; line-height: 1.35; }
    .quiz-choice:hover:not(:disabled) { border-color: rgba(74,158,255,0.4); color: var(--white); background: rgba(74,158,255,0.08); }
    .quiz-choice.correct { border-color: #34d399; background: rgba(52,211,153,0.1); color: #6ee7b7; }
    .quiz-choice.wrong { border-color: #f87171; background: rgba(248,113,113,0.08); color: #fca5a5; }
    .quiz-choice:disabled { cursor: default; }
    .quiz-feedback { margin-top: 1rem; padding: 0.85rem 1.1rem; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 0.875rem; line-height: 1.55; display: none; }
    .quiz-feedback.correct { background: rgba(52,211,153,0.08); border: 1px solid rgba(52,211,153,0.2); color: #6ee7b7; }
    .quiz-feedback.wrong { background: rgba(248,113,113,0.06); border: 1px solid rgba(248,113,113,0.2); color: #fca5a5; }
    .quiz-feedback.visible { display: block; }
    .quiz-next { margin-top: 1rem; display: none; }
    .quiz-next.visible { display: block; }
    .quiz-done { text-align: center; padding: 3rem 1rem; display: none; }
    .quiz-done.visible { display: block; }
    .quiz-done h2 { font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 2.2rem; font-weight: 700; color: var(--white); margin-bottom: 0.5rem; }
    .quiz-done .final-score { font-size: 4rem; font-weight: 800; color: var(--accent); line-height: 1; margin: 1rem 0; }
    .quiz-done p { color: var(--silver); font-size: 0.95rem; margin-bottom: 1.5rem; }
    .fc-btn { padding: 0.6rem 1.4rem; border-radius: 8px; font-size: 0.85rem; font-weight: 700; border: 1px solid rgba(74,158,255,0.25); background: rgba(74,158,255,0.08); color: var(--silver); cursor: pointer; font-family: inherit; transition: all 0.18s; }
    .fc-btn:hover { background: rgba(74,158,255,0.18); color: var(--white); }
    .fc-btn.primary { background: var(--accent); border-color: var(--accent); color: #fff; }
    .fc-btn.primary:hover { background: #3a8eef; }

    /* ── Responsive ── */
    @media (max-width: 600px) {
      .fsc-tab { padding: 0.7rem 0.9rem; font-size: 0.75rem; }
      .da-options { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
      .lookup-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
    }

    .bmc-btn{display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:.4rem;background:#FFDD00;color:#000;border-radius:8px;padding:.45rem 1rem;font-weight:700;font-size:.83rem;text-decoration:none;transition:opacity .2s,transform .15s;margin-top:.75rem}.bmc-btn:hover{opacity:.88;transform:translateY(-1px)}
  </style>

.cfm-brand {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  min-width: 130px; flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-brand-logo {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.95rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; letter-spacing: 0.5px; white-space: nowrap;
}
.cfm-brand-logo span { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-on-air {
  font-size: 0.55rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 1.5px;
  text-transform: uppercase; color: #ef4444;
  background: rgba(239,68,68,0.12); border: 1px solid rgba(239,68,68,0.3);
  border-radius: 3px; padding: 0.1rem 0.35rem;
  animation: cfm-pulse 2s ease-in-out infinite;
  transition: color 0.3s, background 0.3s, border-color 0.3s;
}
.cfm-on-air.off-air {
  color: #445; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); border-color: rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  animation: none;
}
@keyframes cfm-pulse { 0%,100% { opacity:1; } 50% { opacity:0.5; } }

.cfm-song-info {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.75rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  min-width: 210px; max-width: 260px; flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-art {
  width: 40px; height: 40px; border-radius: 6px; flex-shrink: 0;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  font-size: 1.2rem;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  transition: background 0.3s;
}
.cfm-meta { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-meta-title {
  font-size: 0.8rem; font-weight: 600; color: #e2e8f0;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-sub {
  font-size: 0.68rem; color: #556; margin-top: 0.1rem;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-meta-genre {
  display: inline-block; font-size: 0.6rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff);
  background: rgba(74,158,255,0.1); border-radius: 3px;
  padding: 0.1rem 0.35rem; margin-top: 0.15rem; letter-spacing: 0.5px;
}
.cfm-heart {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 1rem;
  color: #445; transition: color 0.2s, transform 0.15s; flex-shrink: 0; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-heart.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-heart:hover { transform: scale(1.2); }

.cfm-controls {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1.25rem; border-right: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0.4rem;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: color 0.18s, background 0.18s, transform 0.15s;
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  width: 30px; height: 30px;
}
.cfm-btn:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn {
  width: 38px; height: 38px; font-size: 1rem;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); color: #040d1f;
  border-radius: 50%; transition: all 0.18s;
}
.cfm-btn.cfm-play-btn:hover { transform: scale(1.08); filter: brightness(1.15); }
.cfm-btn.cfm-active { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }

.cfm-progress-zone {
  flex: 1; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.6rem;
  padding: 0 1.1rem; min-width: 0;
}
.cfm-time { font-size: 0.68rem; color: #445; flex-shrink: 0; min-width: 32px; }
.cfm-time.right { text-align: right; }
.cfm-bar-wrap { flex: 1; position: relative; height: 4px; cursor: pointer; }
.cfm-bar-bg {
  position: absolute; inset: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
}
.cfm-bar-fill {
  position: absolute; left: 0; top: 0; bottom: 0; border-radius: 4px;
  background: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); width: 0%; transition: width 0.1s linear;
}
.cfm-bar-thumb {
  position: absolute; top: 50%; width: 12px; height: 12px;
  border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);
  opacity: 0; transition: opacity 0.18s; box-shadow: 0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.4);
  left: 0%;
}
.cfm-bar-wrap:hover .cfm-bar-thumb { opacity: 1; }

.cfm-volume-zone {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.5rem;
  padding: 0 1rem; border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06); flex-shrink: 0;
}
.cfm-vol-icon { font-size: 0.75rem; color: #445; cursor: pointer; }
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider {
  -webkit-appearance: none; appearance: none;
  width: 70px; height: 3px; border-radius: 3px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); outline: none; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-webkit-slider-thumb {
  -webkit-appearance: none; width: 16px; height: 16px; border-radius: 50%;
  background: #fff; cursor: pointer;
}
input[type=range].cfm-vol-slider::-moz-range-thumb {
  width: 12px; height: 12px; border-radius: 50%; background: #fff; cursor: pointer; border: none;
}

.cfm-playlist-btn {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer;
  color: #8a9bb0; font-size: 0.85rem; padding: 0 1rem;
  transition: color 0.18s; flex-shrink: 0; height: 100%;
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.35rem; font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-playlist-btn:hover { color: #fff; }
.cfm-playlist-btn.open { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-playlist-text { font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; }
.cfm-playlist-count {
  display: inline-grid; place-items: center;
  min-width: 1.35rem; height: 1.35rem; padding: 0 0.28rem;
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  font-size: 0.68rem; font-weight: 800;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle {
  position: relative;
  height: 100%;
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  justify-content: center;
  padding: 0 0.85rem;
  border: none;
  border-left: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
  background: rgba(217,154,49,0.04);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  flex-shrink: 0;
  font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle span {
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.28);
  border-radius: 999px;
  padding: 0.22rem 0.52rem;
  color: #d99a31;
  font-size: 0.68rem;
  font-weight: 900;
  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover span,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible span,
.cfm-cco-toggle.active span {
  color: #080905;
  background: #d99a31;
  border-color: #d99a31;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after {
  content: attr(data-tip);
  position: absolute;
  right: 0.5rem;
  bottom: calc(100% + 10px);
  width: min(300px, calc(100vw - 24px));
  padding: 0.65rem 0.75rem;
  border: 1px solid rgba(217,154,49,0.34);
  border-radius: 8px;
  background: rgba(6,3,16,0.96);
  color: #dbe8f7;
  box-shadow: 0 14px 34px rgba(0,0,0,0.42);
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 650;
  line-height: 1.45;
  opacity: 0;
  pointer-events: none;
  transform: translateY(4px);
  transition: opacity 0.16s ease, transform 0.16s ease;
}
.cfm-cco-toggle:hover::after,
.cfm-cco-toggle:focus-visible::after {
  opacity: 1;
  transform: translateY(0);
}
.cfm-cco-toggle::after,
.cfm-sb-cco-toggle::after {
  content: none !important;
  display: none !important;
}

/* Playlist drawer */
#cfm-drawer {
  position: fixed; bottom: 68px; right: 0;
  width: 380px; max-height: min(560px, calc(100vh - 92px));
  background: #080414;
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.08);
  border-radius: 14px 0 0 0;
  overflow-y: auto; z-index: 9998;
  display: none;
  box-shadow: -4px -4px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.5);
}
#cfm-drawer.open { display: block; }
.cfm-drawer-hdr {
  position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 1;
  padding: 0.85rem 1rem 0.75rem;
  background: #080414;
  border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.06);
}
.cfm-drawer-title-row {
  display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: 0.75rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-title {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 1rem; font-weight: 700;
  color: #fff; text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: 1.2px;
}
.cfm-drawer-count { color: #556; font-size: 0.72rem; font-weight: 700; white-space: nowrap; }
.cfm-drawer-actions {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 0.45rem; margin-top: 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #8a9bb0;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.72rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  padding: 0.35rem 0.65rem;
}
.cfm-drawer-toggle:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.06); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.active { color: #ef4444; border-color: rgba(239,68,68,0.34); background: rgba(239,68,68,0.08); }
.cfm-drawer-toggle.disabled { opacity: 0.45; cursor: default; }
.cfm-drawer-empty {
  padding: 1rem;
  color: #8a9bb0;
  font-size: 0.82rem;
  line-height: 1.55;
}
.cfm-track-item {
  display: grid; grid-template-columns: 22px minmax(0, 1fr) auto auto; align-items: center; gap: 0.65rem;
  padding: 0.65rem 1rem; cursor: pointer;
  background: #080414;
  transition: background 0.15s; border-bottom: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.04);
}
.cfm-track-item:hover { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.04); }
.cfm-track-item.active { background: #11172d; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped { opacity: 0.58; }
.cfm-track-item.skipped .cfm-track-name { text-decoration: line-through; }
.cfm-track-marker {
  display: grid; place-items: center;
  width: 22px; min-width: 22px;
}
.cfm-track-num {
  font-family: 'Rajdhani', sans-serif; font-size: 0.8rem; color: #334;
  min-width: 18px; text-align: center;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-num { color: var(--cfm-accent, #4a9eff); }
.cfm-track-dot {
  width: 8px; height: 8px; border-radius: 50%;
  animation: cfm-pulse 1s ease-in-out infinite; flex-shrink: 0;
  display: none;
}
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-dot { display: block; }
.cfm-track-item.playing .cfm-track-num { display: none; }
.cfm-track-info { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }
.cfm-track-name {
  font-size: 0.82rem; font-weight: 600; color: #c0cdd8;
  white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
.cfm-track-item.active .cfm-track-name { color: #fff; }
.cfm-track-genre { font-size: 0.67rem; color: #445; margin-top: 0.1rem; }
.cfm-track-fav {
  background: none; border: none; cursor: pointer; font-size: 0.85rem;
  color: #334; transition: color 0.18s; padding: 0.2rem;
}
.cfm-track-fav.active { color: #ef4444; }
.cfm-track-skip {
  border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.1);
  border-radius: 999px;
  background: rgba(255,255,255,0.035);
  color: #66758a;
  cursor: pointer;
  font: inherit;
  font-size: 0.64rem;
  font-weight: 800;
  line-height: 1;
  padding: 0.32rem 0.48rem;
  text-transform: uppercase;
}
.cfm-track-skip:hover { color: #fff; background: rgba(255,255,255,0.07); }
.cfm-track-skip.active { color: #f59e0b; border-color: rgba(245,158,11,0.34); background: rgba(245,158,11,0.08); }

/* Scrollbar styling for drawer */
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar { width: 4px; }
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar-track { background: transparent; }
#cfm-drawer::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb { background: rgba(255,255,255,0.1); border-radius: 2px; }

/* Body padding to account for player */
body.has-cfm-player { padding-bottom: 68px; }

<div class="page-hero">
  <div class="container">
    <span class="hero-badge">Beginner Track • Topic 4</span>
    <h1 class="page-hero-title">PSC / FSC Codes</h1>
    <p class="page-hero-sub">PSC/FSC codes tell FPDS what the Government bought. They're simpler than NAICS — but you still need to pick the right one.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="fsc-bg">
  <div class="fsc-tabs" role="tablist">
    <button class="fsc-tab active" data-tab="learn" role="tab">📚 Learn</button>
    <button class="fsc-tab" data-tab="decide" role="tab">🧮 Decision Aid</button>
    <button class="fsc-tab" data-tab="quiz" role="tab">⚡ Quiz</button>
    <button class="fsc-tab" data-tab="lookup" role="tab">🔍 Look It Up</button>
  </div>

  <!-- ═══════════════════════════════════ LEARN ═══ -->
  <div id="panel-learn" class="fsc-panel active">
    <div class="fsc-intro">
      <div class="fsc-intro-tag">The Basics</div>
      <h2>What You Need to Know</h2>
      <p>PSC/FSC codes are reporting codes — they classify what the Government bought so agencies can track spend, spot trends, and build smarter contract strategies.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- Section 1 -->
    <div class="learn-section">
      <h3><span class="section-num">1</span> What is a PSC/FSC Code?</h3>
      <div class="learn-body">
        <p>At the simplest level, a PSC/FSC code tells FPDS <strong>what the Government bought</strong>. That's it.</p>
        <p><strong>PSC</strong> stands for <strong>Product and Service Code</strong>. It's the four-character code reported in FPDS for products, services, and R&D actions. <strong>FSC</strong> stands for <strong>Federal Supply Class</strong> — the product-side classification structure. In practice, people often say "FSC" when they mean products, but the field reported in FPDS is always the PSC field.</p>

        <div class="highlight-box tip">
          <strong>Easy distinction:</strong> NAICS describes the <em>industry</em>. PSC/FSC describes the <em>thing</em> the Government bought. They're different fields but they should tell a consistent story about the acquisition.
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <hr class="learn-divider">

    <!-- Section 2 -->
    <div class="learn-section">
      <h3><span class="section-num">2</span> Why Does It Matter?</h3>
      <div class="learn-body">
        <p>PSC/FSC matters because it helps the Government group similar purchases together for <strong>reporting and spend analysis</strong>. That data lets agencies see buying patterns across offices and across time.</p>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>Downstream impact:</strong> When the Government notices agencies buying the same thing over and over, that data can justify building better contract vehicles — IDIQs, BPAs, or requirements-type contracts. PSC/FSC doesn't drive your day-to-day work, but it feeds the analysis that drives acquisition strategy at the enterprise level.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box warn">
          <strong>What it does NOT do:</strong> PSC/FSC does not replace NAICS, does not determine a small business size standard, and does not by itself decide whether something should be set aside. It's a reporting classification, not a competitive tool.
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <hr class="learn-divider">

    <!-- Section 3 -->
    <div class="learn-section">
      <h3><span class="section-num">3</span> How the Codes Are Structured</h3>
      <div class="learn-body">
        <p>PSC codes are four characters. The first character tells you whether it's a product, service, or R&D buy:</p>

        <div class="highlight-box tip">
          <strong>Products:</strong> First two digits are numeric (e.g., <strong>7110</strong> — Office Furniture, <strong>5510</strong> — Lumber). These come from the Federal Supply Classification system, which is why people call them FSC codes.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>Services:</strong> First character is a letter (e.g., <strong>S201</strong> — Custodial-Janitorial, <strong>D302</strong> — IT Systems Development, <strong>R425</strong> — Engineering & Technical Services). The letter groups them by service category.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>R&D:</strong> Codes beginning with <strong>A</strong> through <strong>A</strong> series cover Research & Development. These are further subdivided by scientific discipline and stage of development.
        </div>

        <p>You don't need to memorize the structure. You just need to know it exists so you can navigate the PSC Manual efficiently.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <hr class="learn-divider">

    <!-- Section 4 -->
    <div class="learn-section">
      <h3><span class="section-num">4</span> How to Pick the Right Code</h3>
      <div class="learn-body">
        <p>Use the same question every time: <strong>What is the principal thing the Government is buying?</strong> Start there. Don't start with the vendor. Don't start with the office asking for it. Start with the requirement.</p>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>Step 1: Separate product from service.</strong> If you're buying chairs, batteries, laptops, or parts — you're on the product side. If you're buying janitorial support, help desk support, or consulting — you're on the service side.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>Step 2: Go with the predominant purpose.</strong> If the buy includes more than one thing, use the code that best represents the predominant dollars or principal purpose. A purchase order with $1,000 of lumber and $500 of pipe? Code it under lumber.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box tip">
          <strong>Step 3: Check alignment with NAICS.</strong> Your PSC/FSC and NAICS code are different fields, but they should not tell conflicting stories. If your NAICS says you're buying IT services but your PSC says you're buying office furniture, something is wrong.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box warn">
          <strong>Step 4: Don't overthink it.</strong> It's important to pick a reasonable code, but you don't need to spend hours questioning whether you got the perfect PSC/FSC. Make a supportable call and keep the acquisition moving.
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <hr class="learn-divider">

    <!-- Section 5 -->
    <div class="learn-section">
      <h3><span class="section-num">5</span> PSC vs. NAICS: The Quick Comparison</h3>
      <div class="learn-body">
        <p>PSC and NAICS are easy to mix up. Here's the simplest way to keep them straight:</p>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>NAICS</strong> answers: "What industry does the work?" It's six digits, set by SBA, and determines the small business size standard. NAICS is a competitive tool — it affects who can bid as small business.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box">
          <strong>PSC/FSC</strong> answers: "What did the Government buy?" It's four characters, maintained by GSA, and is primarily used for FPDS reporting. PSC/FSC is a reporting tool — it helps agencies track and analyze their spend data.
        </div>

        <div class="highlight-box tip">
          <strong>Bottom line:</strong> NAICS selection is a bigger deal because it's protestable and drives set-asides. PSC/FSC selection is simpler — but still needs to accurately describe the purchase. Both should be consistent with each other and with the requirement.
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- ═══════════════════════════════════ DECISION AID ═══ -->
  <div id="panel-decide" class="fsc-panel">
    <div class="fsc-intro">
      <div class="fsc-intro-tag">Interactive</div>
      <h2>PSC/FSC Decision Aid</h2>
      <p>Tell us what you're buying and get guidance on which PSC category to start with.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="da-prompt">
      <h3>What are you buying?</h3>
      <p>Select the category that best describes the principal thing being purchased.</p>
    </div>

    <div class="da-options" id="daOptions">
      <div class="da-option" data-type="product" tabindex="0" role="button">
        <span class="da-option-icon">📦</span>
        <div class="da-option-label">A Product</div>
        <div class="da-option-sub">Supplies, equipment, materials — something tangible that you receive</div>
      </div>
      <div class="da-option" data-type="service" tabindex="0" role="button">
        <span class="da-option-icon">🛠</span>
        <div class="da-option-label">A Service</div>
        <div class="da-option-sub">Someone performing work — IT, janitorial, consulting, maintenance</div>
      </div>
      <div class="da-option" data-type="randd" tabindex="0" role="button">
        <span class="da-option-icon">🔬</span>
        <div class="da-option-label">R&D</div>
        <div class="da-option-sub">Research and development — basic research, applied research, or development</div>
      </div>
      <div class="da-option" data-type="mixed" tabindex="0" role="button">
        <span class="da-option-icon">🔄</span>
        <div class="da-option-label">Mixed Buy</div>
        <div class="da-option-sub">Combination of products and services on the same action</div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Product result -->
    <div class="da-result" id="result-product">
      <h4>📦 Buying a Product (Supply)</h4>
      <p>Product PSC codes are <strong>four-digit numeric codes</strong> based on the Federal Supply Classification. The first two digits identify the commodity group.</p>
      <p>Common product groups you'll see:</p>
      <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:0.5rem;margin:0.75rem 0 1rem;">
        <span class="da-series">71xx — Furniture</span>
        <span class="da-series">70xx — IT Equipment</span>
        <span class="da-series">55xx — Lumber</span>
        <span class="da-series">85xx — Toiletries</span>
        <span class="da-series">13xx — Ammunition</span>
        <span class="da-series">66xx — Instruments</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>How to find yours:</strong> Open the PSC Manual, look up the Federal Supply Group that matches what you're buying, then narrow to the four-digit class that fits best.</p>
      <div class="da-caution">
        <strong>Don't use the customer's casual label.</strong> If someone calls their purchase "office support" but they're buying chairs, the PSC is 7110 (Office Furniture), not a services code. Code the thing being bought, not what someone called it.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Service result -->
    <div class="da-result" id="result-service">
      <h4>🛠 Buying a Service</h4>
      <p>Service PSC codes start with a <strong>letter</strong> followed by three digits. The letter tells you the service category.</p>
      <p>Common service series:</p>
      <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:0.5rem;margin:0.75rem 0 1rem;">
        <span class="da-series">D — IT & Telecom</span>
        <span class="da-series">R — Professional Services</span>
        <span class="da-series">S — Utilities & Housekeeping</span>
        <span class="da-series">J — Maintenance & Repair</span>
        <span class="da-series">B — Special Studies</span>
        <span class="da-series">Z — Construction (minor)</span>
      </div>
      <p><strong>Focus on the work being performed.</strong> If the contractor is cleaning a building, that's S201 (Custodial-Janitorial), even if the contract includes some cleaning supplies. The supplies are incidental — the principal purpose is the service.</p>
      <div class="da-caution">
        <strong>Watch for construction overlap.</strong> Minor construction, alteration, and repair work uses PSC codes in the Z series. Major construction projects use Y-series codes. Make sure you're in the right series for the scope of work.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- R&D result -->
    <div class="da-result" id="result-randd">
      <h4>🔬 Research & Development</h4>
      <p>R&D PSC codes use the <strong>A series</strong>. They're organized by scientific discipline and development stage.</p>
      <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:0.5rem;margin:0.75rem 0 1rem;">
        <span class="da-series">A — R&D (all stages)</span>
      </div>
      <p>The second character of an R&D PSC often identifies the development stage: basic research, applied research, advanced development, or operational systems development. The remaining digits specify the scientific or technical discipline.</p>
      <p><strong>Key distinction:</strong> R&D codes are for actual research and development activities. If you're buying IT services that support an R&D program but the contractor is providing help desk support, that's still a D-series service code, not an A-series R&D code.</p>
      <div class="da-caution">
        <strong>Match the work, not the program.</strong> Just because the funding comes from an R&D budget doesn't mean the PSC should be R&D. Code the nature of the work being performed.
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Mixed result -->
    <div class="da-result" id="result-mixed">
      <h4>🔄 Mixed Buy</h4>
      <p>When a purchase includes both products and services, use the PSC that matches the <strong>predominant purpose</strong> of the acquisition.</p>
      <p>Ask: <strong>Where are most of the dollars going?</strong> If 70% of the spend is on the service and 30% is on supplies that support the service, code it as a service. If 80% is a product purchase with some installation labor, code it as a product.</p>
      <div class="da-caution">
        <strong>Don't split the PSC.</strong> FPDS takes one PSC per contract action. You're picking the single code that best represents the principal purpose. When in doubt, go with the predominant dollar value.
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="da-reset" id="daReset">
      <button onclick="resetDecisionAid()">← Start Over</button>
    </div>
  </div>

      <div class="quiz-choices" id="quizChoices"><button class="quiz-choice" data-idx="0">S201 — Custodial-Janitorial</button><button class="quiz-choice" data-idx="1">7110 — Office Furniture</button><button class="quiz-choice" data-idx="2">D399 — Other IT Services</button><button class="quiz-choice" data-idx="3">R499 — Other Professional Services</button></div>
      <div class="quiz-feedback" id="quizFeedback"></div>

  <!-- ═══════════════════════════════════ LOOK IT UP ═══ -->

      <h2>Look It Up</h2>

    </div>

    <div class="lookup-grid">
      <div class="lookup-card">
        <h4>PSC Manual</h4>
        <p>The official source for current Product and Service Codes. This is your primary reference when you need the actual code list and descriptions.</p>
        <a href="https://www.acquisition.gov/psc-manual" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open the PSC Manual</a>
      </div>
      <div class="lookup-card">
        <h4>PSC Tool</h4>
        <p>A practical search tool that narrows PSC/FSC options based on keywords or the NAICS code you've already selected. Great for cross-referencing.</p>
        <a href="https://psctool.us/home" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open PSC Tool</a>
      </div>
      <div class="lookup-card">
        <h4>FPDS PSC Reference</h4>

      <div class="lookup-card">
        <h4>GSA Federal Supply Classes</h4>

      <div class="lookup-card">
        <h4>USAspending.gov</h4>

        <a href="https://www.usaspending.gov" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Open USAspending</a>
      </div>
    </div>

<script>
/* ═══════════════════════════════════ TABS ═══ */
document.querySelectorAll('.fsc-tab').forEach(tab => {
  tab.addEventListener('click', () => {
    document.querySelectorAll('.fsc-tab').forEach(t => t.classList.remove('active'));
    document.querySelectorAll('.fsc-panel').forEach(p => p.classList.remove('active'));
    tab.classList.add('active');
    document.getElementById('panel-' + tab.dataset.tab).classList.add('active');
  });
});

/* ═══════════════════════════════════ DECISION AID ═══ */
document.querySelectorAll('.da-option').forEach(opt => {
  opt.addEventListener('click', () => selectCategory(opt.dataset.type));
  opt.addEventListener('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') { e.preventDefault(); selectCategory(opt.dataset.type); } });
});

function selectCategory(type) {
  document.querySelectorAll('.da-option').forEach(o => o.classList.remove('selected'));
  document.querySelector(`.da-option[data-type="${type}"]`).classList.add('selected');
  document.querySelectorAll('.da-result').forEach(r => r.classList.remove('visible'));
  document.getElementById('result-' + type).classList.add('visible');
  document.getElementById('daReset').classList.add('visible');
  setTimeout(() => document.getElementById('result-' + type).scrollIntoView({ behavior: 'smooth', block: 'nearest' }), 100);
}

function resetDecisionAid() {
  document.querySelectorAll('.da-option').forEach(o => o.classList.remove('selected'));
  document.querySelectorAll('.da-result').forEach(r => r.classList.remove('visible'));
  document.getElementById('daReset').classList.remove('visible');
}

/* ═══════════════════════════════════ QUIZ ═══ */
const quizData = [
  {
    q: "Your office is buying 60 ergonomic desk chairs for an admin building. The customer keeps calling it an \"office support requirement.\" Which PSC code fits best?",
    choices: ["S201 — Custodial-Janitorial", "7110 — Office Furniture", "D399 — Other IT Services", "R499 — Other Professional Services"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "The principal thing being purchased is furniture — regardless of what the customer casually calls the requirement. Code the thing being bought, not the label someone gave it. PSC 7110 covers Office Furniture."
  },
  {
    q: "You're buying janitorial services for a clinic. The contract includes cleaning supplies, but the contractor's main job is performing recurring cleaning. Which PSC code fits best?",
    choices: ["8520 — Toilet Soap & Cleaning Compounds", "S201 — Custodial-Janitorial", "7110 — Office Furniture", "It doesn't matter since both items are on the contract"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "The cleaning supplies are incidental. The principal purpose of the acquisition is the janitorial service — S201. Always code the predominant purpose, not the incidental items that support it."
  },
  {
    q: "A purchase order includes $1,000 of lumber and $500 of pipe. How do you pick the PSC?",
    choices: ["Use the PSC for lumber since it's the higher dollar value", "Use the PSC for pipe since it was listed second", "Use two PSC codes — one for each item", "It doesn't matter since both are products"],
    correct: 0,
    explanation: "FPDS takes one PSC per contract action. When more than one item is being bought, use the code that matches the predominant product by dollar value. Lumber at $1,000 is the predominant purchase here."
  },
  {
    q: "What is the key difference between NAICS and PSC/FSC?",
    choices: [
      "NAICS is for services, PSC is for products",
      "NAICS describes the industry; PSC/FSC describes what was bought",
      "They're the same thing with different names",
      "NAICS is reported in FPDS, PSC is not"
    ],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "NAICS classifies the industry performing the work. PSC/FSC classifies the thing the Government purchased. Both are reported in FPDS, both apply to products and services, and they're completely different classification systems that should tell a consistent story."
  },
  {
    q: "Your requirement is for IT help desk support on a research lab contract. The funding comes from an R&D budget. How should you pick the PSC?",
    choices: ["Use an R&D code since the funding is R&D", "Use an IT services code since the work being performed is help desk support", "Use a professional services code since it supports research", "It doesn't matter — any of these would be acceptable"],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Code the nature of the work being performed, not the funding source. The contractor is providing IT help desk support. Just because the money comes from an R&D program doesn't change what the contractor is actually doing."
  },
  {
    q: "You're reporting a contract action in FPDS for a buy that includes both a product and installation labor. 80% of the cost is the product, 20% is installation. How do you handle the PSC?",
    choices: [
      "Use two PSC codes — one for the product, one for the service",
      "Always use a service code when any labor is involved",
      "Use the product PSC since it represents the predominant dollar value",
      "Ask the customer which code they prefer"
    ],
    correct: 2,
    explanation: "FPDS takes one PSC per contract action. Use the code that represents the predominant purpose — in this case, 80% of the spend is on the product. The installation labor is incidental to the principal purchase."
  },
  {
    q: "You picked a NAICS code for IT services, but you're about to select a PSC code for office furniture. Is there a problem?",
    choices: [
      "No — NAICS and PSC are independent fields that don't need to align",
      "Yes — your PSC and NAICS should tell a consistent story about what you're buying",
      "No — PSC is just for reporting, so it doesn't matter what you pick",
      "Yes — PSC and NAICS must always be identical codes"
    ],
    correct: 1,
    explanation: "Your PSC and NAICS are different classification systems, but they should not tell conflicting stories. If your NAICS says IT services but your PSC says office furniture, something is wrong with one of your selections. They don't need to be identical, but they need to be consistent."
  }
];

let currentQ = 0, score = 0, answered = false;

function renderQuestion() {
  if (currentQ >= quizData.length) { showResults(); return; }
  const q = quizData[currentQ];
  answered = false;
  document.getElementById('quizQuestion').innerHTML = `<div class="quiz-question"><div class="quiz-q-label">Scenario ${currentQ + 1}</div><div class="quiz-q-text">${q.q}</div></div>`;
  const choicesEl = document.getElementById('quizChoices');
  choicesEl.innerHTML = q.choices.map((c, i) => `<button class="quiz-choice" data-idx="${i}">${c}</button>`).join('');
  choicesEl.querySelectorAll('.quiz-choice').forEach(btn => btn.addEventListener('click', () => handleAnswer(parseInt(btn.dataset.idx))));
  document.getElementById('quizFeedback').classList.remove('visible', 'correct', 'wrong');
  document.getElementById('quizNext').classList.remove('visible');
  document.getElementById('quizProgress').textContent = `Question ${currentQ + 1} of ${quizData.length}`;
  document.getElementById('quizBar').style.width = ((currentQ) / quizData.length * 100) + '%';
  document.getElementById('quizScore').textContent = `Score: ${score} / ${currentQ}`;
}

function handleAnswer(idx) {
  if (answered) return;
  answered = true;
  const q = quizData[currentQ];
  const btns = document.querySelectorAll('#quizChoices .quiz-choice');
  btns.forEach(b => { b.disabled = true; });
  btns[q.correct].classList.add('correct');
  const fb = document.getElementById('quizFeedback');
  if (idx === q.correct) {
    score++;
    fb.className = 'quiz-feedback visible correct';
    fb.textContent = '\u2713 Correct. ' + q.explanation;
  } else {
    btns[idx].classList.add('wrong');
    fb.className = 'quiz-feedback visible wrong';
    fb.textContent = '\u2717 Not quite. ' + q.explanation;
  }
  document.getElementById('quizScore').textContent = `Score: ${score} / ${currentQ + 1}`;
  document.getElementById('quizBar').style.width = ((currentQ + 1) / quizData.length * 100) + '%';
  document.getElementById('quizNext').classList.add('visible');
}

function nextQuestion() {
  currentQ++;
  renderQuestion();
}

function showResults() {
  document.getElementById('quizContainer').style.display = 'none';
  const pct = Math.round(score / quizData.length * 100);
  document.getElementById('finalScore').textContent = pct + '%';
  document.getElementById('finalMsg').textContent = pct === 100 ? "Perfect. You know your PSC codes." : pct >= 67 ? "Solid foundation. Review the ones you missed." : "Worth another pass through the Learn tab before reporting your next contract action.";
  document.getElementById('quizDone').classList.add('visible');
}

function restartQuiz() {
  currentQ = 0; score = 0;
  document.getElementById('quizContainer').style.display = 'block';
  document.getElementById('quizDone').classList.remove('visible');
  renderQuestion();
}

// Initialize quiz
renderQuestion();
</script>
